saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The reforming Bishop of Grenoble who welcomed St. Bruno and gave the Carthusians their first home…
biography: Born near Valence about 1053, Hugh was made Bishop of Grenoble in 1080 while still a young man, and he governed the diocese for more than fifty years. He set himself against simony and the moral laxity of the clergy, restored the discipline and finances of his see, and twice tried to resign for the solitude of monastic life, only to be sent back to his duties by the pope.

In 1084 he received St. Bruno and his six companions and granted them the wild valley of the Chartreuse, where they founded the first house of the Carthusian Order; Hugh remained its lifelong friend and protector. Worn out by austerity and long labour, he died in 1132 and was canonized only two years later by Pope Innocent II.
saints.knownFor: Reforming his diocese and giving the Carthusians the valley of the Chartreuse.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 1 April

saints.name: St. Francis of Paola
saints.title: Hermit and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A Calabrian hermit whose penance and miracles founded the Order of Minims, the “least” of religious…
biography: Born at Paola in Calabria in 1416, Francis withdrew as a youth to a cave on the seashore to live as a hermit. Disciples gathered around his austerity, and from them grew the Order of Minims — so named to mark them as the “least” in the household of God — who added to the usual vows a perpetual Lenten abstinence from all flesh and dairy.

Renowned for prophecy and healing, he was summoned to France by the dying King Louis XI, who hoped for a cure; Francis instead prepared the king for a holy death and remained at the French court as a counsellor to his successors. He died at Plessis-les-Tours in 1507 and was canonized by Pope Leo X in 1519. Because of a tradition that he once crossed the Strait of Messina on his spread cloak, he is honoured as a patron of seafarers.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Order of Minims and a life of extreme penance.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 2 April

saints.name: St. Richard of Chichester
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The devoted Bishop of Chichester whose prayer still asks to know, love, and follow Christ more nearly…
biography: Richard de Wych was born about 1197 at Droitwich in England, rebuilt his family's ruined estate by his own labour, and then gave himself to study at Oxford, Paris, and Bologna. He served St. Edmund of Abingdon as chancellor and, after Edmund's death, was chosen Bishop of Chichester in 1244 — a choice King Henry III resisted, seizing the diocese's revenues so that Richard lived for two years on the charity of his people.

As bishop he was a model of pastoral zeal and personal poverty, exact in almsgiving and firm in reforming his clergy. He died at Dover in 1253 while preaching a crusade and was canonized in 1262. The prayer traditionally ascribed to him — to know Christ more clearly, love him more dearly, and follow him more nearly — has remained a treasure of English devotion.
saints.knownFor: His pastoral holiness and the prayer that bears his name.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 3 April

saints.name: St. Isidore of Seville
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The last of the Latin Fathers, whose learning gathered the wisdom of the ancient world for a new age…
biography: Born at Cartagena about 560 into a family that gave the Church four saints, Isidore succeeded his brother Leander as Archbishop of Seville around the year 600. He completed the conversion of the Visigoths of Spain from Arianism and presided over councils, chief among them the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, which ordered a school in every diocese.

Isidore is best remembered as an encyclopaedist: his Etymologies gathered and preserved the learning of the ancient world for the medieval West, and his historical and theological works were read for centuries. Often called the last of the Latin Fathers, he died in 636 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1722; because his great work sought to organize all knowledge, he is popularly proposed as a patron of students and the Internet.
saints.knownFor: His Etymologies and his labour to preserve ancient learning.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1722)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 April

saints.name: St. Vincent Ferrer
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Dominican “Angel of the Judgment,” whose preaching of penance stirred all of Western Europe…
biography: Born at Valencia about 1350, Vincent entered the Order of Preachers and became a theologian of note, but it was as a wandering preacher that he gained his fame. For twenty years he crossed Spain, France, Italy, and beyond, drawing vast crowds with sermons on sin, death, and the coming judgment, and reconciling multitudes of sinners, Jews, and Muslims to the faith.

He lived through the Western Schism and long supported the Avignon claimant Benedict XIII, whom he had known personally; but when Benedict refused to yield for the sake of unity, Vincent publicly withdrew his obedience, helping open the way to the Church's reunion at the Council of Constance. He died at Vannes in Brittany in 1419 and was canonized in 1455.
saints.knownFor: His preaching of repentance and his part in healing the Western Schism.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 April

saints.name: Pope St. Celestine I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who upheld the title Mother of God at Ephesus and sent the faith toward Britain and Ireland…
biography: Celestine was elected Bishop of Rome in 422 and governed the Church through a decade marked by great doctrinal struggles. He condemned the errors of Pelagius on grace and, above all, threw the weight of Rome against Nestorius of Constantinople, whose teaching seemed to divide Christ; Celestine's judgment guided the Council of Ephesus in 431, which proclaimed the Blessed Virgin truly Theotokos, the Mother of God.

His care reached the edges of the known world: he sent St. Germanus of Auxerre to combat heresy in Britain and, by tradition, dispatched the deacon Palladius as first bishop to the Christians of Ireland, shortly before St. Patrick. He died in 432 and has been venerated as a saint from antiquity.
saints.knownFor: Backing the Council of Ephesus and the defence of Mary as Mother of God.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 6 April

saints.name: St. John Baptist de la Salle
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A French canon who gave up rank and wealth to found free schools and train the teachers of the poor…
biography: Born to a wealthy family at Reims in 1651 and ordained a priest and cathedral canon, John Baptist de la Salle turned from a comfortable ecclesiastical career to the education of poor and working-class boys. Step by step he gathered lay schoolmasters into a community, resigned his canonry, gave away his fortune during a famine, and bound himself to the men he was forming.

From this beginning grew the Brothers of the Christian Schools, the first Catholic teaching order of laymen vowed to gratuitous popular education. He pioneered the training of teachers, classroom teaching in the vernacular, and instruction in groups rather than one by one. Worn out by opposition and toil, he died in 1719, was canonized in 1900, and in 1950 was declared the heavenly patron of all who teach the young.
saints.knownFor: Founding the De La Salle Brothers and modern teacher training.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John Baptist de la Salle”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 April

saints.name: St. Julie Billiart
saints.title: Virgin and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A French peasant woman, long paralyzed, who rose to found the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur…
biography: Julie Billiart was born in 1751 at Cuvilly in Picardy, a farmer's daughter who taught catechism from childhood. A shock left her progressively paralyzed for some twenty-two years, much of it spent bedridden, yet she continued to instruct and to shelter hunted priests during the French Revolution.

In 1804, at Amiens, she founded with the Viscountess Françoise Blin de Bourdon the Institute of the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur, devoted to the Christian education of poor girls; in that same year, in answer to a novena, she was suddenly and completely healed. Her motto, “How good is the good God,” marked a life of great trust. She died at Namur in 1816, was beatified in 1906, and canonized in 1969.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur for the education of poor girls.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Julie Billiart (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Waltrude
saints.title: Abbess
saints.shortBlurb: A noblewoman of Hainaut whose convent became the seed of the city of Mons…
biography: Waltrude — Waudru in French — was a seventh-century noblewoman of Hainaut, daughter, wife, and mother of saints; her sister was St. Aldegonde and her husband St. Vincent Madelgarus, and their four children were also venerated as saints. After her husband withdrew to become a monk, Waltrude gave herself to prayer and charity.

She founded a small convent on a hill, around which a settlement grew that became the city of Mons in present-day Belgium. Renowned for her care of the poor and the sick, she died about 688 and is honoured as the principal patron of Mons, where her relics are still carried in a yearly procession.
saints.knownFor: Founding the community that grew into the city of Mons.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 9 April

saints.name: St. Fulbert of Chartres
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop and teacher who made Chartres a beacon of learning and rebuilt its great cathedral…
biography: Fulbert was born about 960 and studied under Gerbert of Aurillac, the future Pope Sylvester II. As master of the cathedral school of Chartres he made it one of the foremost centres of learning in Europe, drawing students from many lands and earning the affectionate title of “venerable Socrates” from his pupils.

Chosen Bishop of Chartres in 1006, he was a wise and charitable pastor, a counsellor to kings, and a firm opponent of abuses. When his cathedral burned in 1020 he began the great rebuilding whose crypt survives to this day. Devoted to the Blessed Virgin, he composed sermons and hymns in her honour, especially for the feast of her Nativity, and died in 1028.
saints.knownFor: The school of Chartres and the rebuilding of its cathedral.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 10 April

saints.name: St. Stanislaus
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The Bishop of Kraków slain at the altar for rebuking a king, and the patron of Poland…
biography: Stanislaus was born in 1030 at Szczepanów and became Bishop of Kraków in 1072. A zealous pastor, he did not shrink from confronting King Bolesław II the Bold over his cruelties and injustices, at last excommunicating the king when he would not amend.

Enraged, Bolesław ordered the bishop killed, and by tradition he himself struck Stanislaus down while the saint was celebrating Mass in a chapel outside the city in 1079. Venerated at once as a martyr, Stanislaus was canonized in 1253 and became a symbol of the Polish nation and the moral authority of its bishops; he is honoured as a principal patron of Poland.
saints.knownFor: Dying a martyr for the Church's freedom against a king.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 April

saints.name: Pope St. Julius I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who sheltered St. Athanasius and stood for Nicaea against the Arian tide…
biography: Julius I was elected Bishop of Rome in 337, in the thick of the Arian controversy that followed the Council of Nicaea. When St. Athanasius of Alexandria was driven from his see by the Arians, Julius received him at Rome, examined his cause, and declared him innocent, upholding the appeal of an eastern bishop to the See of Peter.

He convened a Roman synod about 340 to vindicate Athanasius and pressed for the wider Council of Sardica, defending both the Nicene faith and the rights of the Roman See. He died in 352 and is venerated as a saint; a tradition credits him with helping to fix the celebration of Christ's Nativity on the twenty-fifth of December.
saints.knownFor: Defending St. Athanasius and the Nicene faith against Arianism.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 12 April

saints.name: Pope St. Martin I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The last pope to die a martyr, exiled and starved for condemning heresy about Christ's will…
biography: Martin I became pope in 649 and at once summoned the Lateran Synod, which condemned Monothelitism — the teaching that Christ had only one will — and rejected the imperial edict that forbade the dispute. This defiance of Constantinople enraged the Emperor Constans II.

Martin was seized in Rome, carried off to the imperial capital, tried, publicly humiliated, and condemned; his sentence was commuted to exile in the Crimea, where hunger and hardship soon killed him in 655. He is honoured as the last of the popes venerated by the Church as a martyr.
saints.knownFor: Condemning Monothelitism and dying in exile for the faith.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 April

saints.name: St. Lidwina of Schiedam
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A Dutch maiden whose thirty-eight years of illness became a school of redemptive suffering…
biography: Lidwina was born at Schiedam in Holland in 1380. At about fifteen she fell while ice-skating and broke a rib; the injury never healed, and she passed the rest of her life bedridden, her body wracked by an illness that grew ever more grievous over some thirty-eight years.

Rather than despair, Lidwina offered her sufferings for sinners and for the Church, was granted visions and a deep union with the Passion, and in her later years is said to have taken almost no food but the Eucharist. Widely revered in her own lifetime, she died in 1433; her cult was confirmed by Pope Leo XIII in 1890, and she is invoked as a patron of the chronically ill.
saints.knownFor: Bearing long illness as an offering of redemptive suffering.

canonization.canonized: Cult confirmed 1890 by Pope Leo XIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 14 April

saints.name: St. Hunna
saints.title: Matron
saints.shortBlurb: A noblewoman of Alsace called “the Holy Washerwoman” for washing the clothes of the poor with her own hands…
biography: Hunna was a noblewoman of Alsace, wife of a nobleman of the region of Strasbourg, who lived in the seventh century. Moved by charity, she took upon herself the humblest services to the poor of her district, and because she washed the clothing of the needy with her own hands she came to be known as “the Holy Washerwoman.”

She was guided in the spiritual life by St. Deodatus (Dé), Bishop of Nevers, who had settled in the Vosges. She died about 679, and her memory endured in Alsace until she was formally canonized by Pope Leo XIII in 1877; she is invoked as a patron of laundresses.
saints.knownFor: Serving the poor by washing their clothes with her own hands.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 15 April
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 April

saints.name: St. Bernadette Soubirous
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The poor miller's daughter of Lourdes to whom the Immaculate Conception appeared…
biography: Marie-Bernarde “Bernadette” Soubirous was born in 1844 into a poor family at Lourdes in the French Pyrenees. In 1858, when she was fourteen, a lady appeared to her eighteen times in the grotto of Massabielle; asked her name, the lady said, “I am the Immaculate Conception,” and a spring welled up that became a place of countless healings.

Simple, unlettered, and often doubted, Bernadette bore the questioning of Church and civil authorities with patience, and later entered the Sisters of Charity at Nevers, where she lived hidden and in poor health until her death in 1879. She was canonized in 1933 — not for the visions, the Church was careful to say, but for the humility and faith of her whole life.
saints.knownFor: The apparitions of Our Lady of Lourdes and her hidden holiness.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Bernadette Soubirous (vatican.va)

saints.name: Pope St. Anicetus
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An early pope who received St. Polycarp and kept charity amid the dispute over Easter…
biography: Anicetus was Bishop of Rome in the middle of the second century, in an age when the young Church contended with heresy and awaited persecution. He resisted the Gnostics and, according to ancient testimony, welcomed to Rome the aged St. Polycarp of Smyrna, disciple of the Apostle John.

The two discussed the differing customs for keeping Easter — the churches of Asia observing it with the Jewish Passover, Rome on the Sunday — and though they could not agree, they parted in peace and communion, Anicetus yielding to Polycarp the honour of celebrating the Eucharist. He is numbered among the early popes venerated as martyrs and died about 168.
saints.knownFor: His charity toward St. Polycarp in the early Easter controversy.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 17 April

saints.name: St. Apollonius the Apologist
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A learned Roman senator who defended the faith before the Senate and died for it…
biography: Apollonius was a Roman of rank and learning, said to be a senator, who lived in the reign of Emperor Commodus. Denounced as a Christian by one of his own servants, he was brought before the authorities and, rather than deny his faith, delivered a reasoned defense of Christianity before the Senate and the prefect Perennis.

His apology, praised by the early historian Eusebius, could not save him under the standing laws against Christians, and he was condemned and beheaded about the year 185. He stands among the earliest of the educated Roman martyrs who answered persecution with a public account of their belief.
saints.knownFor: His reasoned defense of the faith before the Roman Senate.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 18 April

saints.name: St. Alphege of Canterbury
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An archbishop who forbade his own ransom and was slain by Danish raiders…
biography: Alphege — Ælfheah in Old English — was a monk and hermit who became Bishop of Winchester and, in 1006, Archbishop of Canterbury. When a Danish army sacked Canterbury in 1011, they seized him and held him for a great ransom.

Alphege forbade his impoverished people to pay it, unwilling to buy his life at their cost. Held captive for months, he was murdered by his drunken captors at Greenwich in 1012, pelted with the bones of their feast and finished with a blow of an axe. Honoured at once as a martyr, he was canonized in 1078 and is counted among the great martyrs of the English Church.
saints.knownFor: Refusing to let the poor be taxed for his ransom, and dying at Danish hands.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 April

saints.name: St. Agnes of Montepulciano
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A Tuscan prioress and mystic whom St. Catherine of Siena honoured as a mother in religion…
biography: Agnes was born about 1268 near Montepulciano in Tuscany and entered religious life as a child, so admired for holiness that she was made head of a community while still very young. She later founded a monastery at Montepulciano that came under the Dominican rule, and she governed it as prioress with wisdom and austerity.

Renowned in her lifetime for prayer, penance, and reported miracles, she died in 1317. A century later St. Catherine of Siena venerated her memory and visited her tomb; Agnes was canonized in 1726 by Pope Benedict XIII, himself a Dominican.
saints.knownFor: Her mystical life and her monastery at Montepulciano.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 April

saints.name: St. Anselm of Canterbury
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The father of scholastic theology, who sought faith seeking understanding…
biography: Born at Aosta about 1033, Anselm became a monk at the Abbey of Bec in Normandy, where his brilliance and holiness raised him to prior and then abbot. There he wrote the Monologion and Proslogion, works of prayerful reasoning that gave the West his famous programme, “faith seeking understanding,” and the celebrated argument for the existence of God.

Called to be Archbishop of Canterbury in 1093, he twice went into exile in his long struggle with the English kings over the Church's liberty and the investiture of bishops. His treatise Cur Deus Homo shaped Western thought on the Redemption. He died in 1109 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1720, honoured as a founder of scholastic theology.
saints.knownFor: “Faith seeking understanding” and the birth of scholastic theology.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1720)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 April

saints.name: Sts. Soter and Caius
saints.title: Popes and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two early popes honoured together, one famed for charity and the other for a martyr's blood…
biography: Pope St. Soter governed the Roman Church about the years 166 to 174 and was renowned for his charity, sending generous aid to distant churches; St. Dionysius of Corinth wrote to thank him, praising Rome's ancient custom of helping the brethren everywhere. Soter is also remembered for defending the Church against the Montanist error.

Pope St. Caius, or Gaius, reigned near the end of the third century, dying about 296 on the eve of the great persecution of Diocletian; tradition made him a kinsman of the emperor and honoured him as a martyr. The two popes have long shared this single commemoration in the Roman calendar.
saints.knownFor: Their governance of the early Roman Church and their witness to Christ.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 22 April

saints.name: St. George
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The soldier-martyr of the early Church, honoured across East and West as a model of courage…
biography: George is one of the most venerated martyrs of the early Church, honoured in both East and West from ancient times. Reliable tradition holds that he was a soldier, probably an officer, who was put to death for his faith at Lydda in Palestine during the persecution under Diocletian about the year 303.

The famous legend of the dragon, in which the knight George rescues a maiden and a city, grew up in the Middle Ages as an emblem of the Christian's battle against evil, and made him a favourite patron of soldiers and of chivalry. He is honoured as the patron of England and of many nations and cities.
saints.knownFor: His witness as a soldier-martyr and his patronage of soldiers and England.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 23 April

saints.name: St. Fidelis of Sigmaringen
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A lawyer turned Capuchin, the “advocate of the poor” who died preaching the faith to the Grisons…
biography: Born Mark Rey at Sigmaringen in 1577, he studied law and won such a name for defending the poor without charge that he was called “the advocate of the poor.” Disillusioned by the injustices of the courts, he entered the Capuchin Franciscans, taking the name Fidelis, and gave away his inheritance to the needy and to poor students.

A tireless preacher and man of penance, he was sent by the newly founded Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith to reconcile the Protestant cantons of the Grisons in Switzerland. His success stirred violent opposition, and in 1622 he was set upon and killed at Seewis for refusing to renounce the Catholic faith — the first martyr of that missionary congregation. He was canonized in 1746.
saints.knownFor: Dying as the first martyr of the missions of Propaganda Fide.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 April

saints.name: St. Mark
saints.title: Evangelist
saints.shortBlurb: The evangelist whose brief, vivid Gospel preserves the preaching of St. Peter, and traditional founder of the Church of Alexandria…
biography: Mark, called also John Mark, was a companion of Paul and Barnabas and a disciple of Peter, whose preaching in Rome he is said to have set down in the shortest and most direct of the four Gospels. Tradition sends him afterward to Egypt, where he founded the Church of Alexandria and was martyred.
His symbol is the winged lion. His relics are venerated at Venice, of which he is the patron.
saints.knownFor: Writing the Gospel that preserves Peter's preaching.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 25 April

saints.name: St. Paschasius Radbertus
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The Benedictine abbot who wrote the first great treatise on the Eucharist…
biography: Paschasius Radbertus was a Benedictine monk and, for a time, abbot of the great monastery of Corbie in Frankish Gaul in the ninth century. A learned theologian and biblical commentator, he lived amid the intellectual revival of the Carolingian age.

His most influential work, On the Body and Blood of the Lord, was the first full systematic treatise on the Eucharist, teaching clearly that the bread and wine become the true Body and Blood of Christ. Though it provoked debate in its own day, it deeply shaped later Catholic doctrine on the Real Presence. He resigned his abbacy to devote himself to study and prayer and died about 865.
saints.knownFor: The first systematic treatise on the Real Presence in the Eucharist.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain), 26 April

saints.name: St. Zita
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A humble maidservant of Lucca who made a lifetime of housework a path to holiness…
biography: Zita was born about 1212 in Tuscany and at the age of twelve entered the service of the wealthy Fatinelli family of Lucca, where she remained a household servant for the rest of her life — some forty-eight years. She rose before dawn to pray and to work, gave her own food and even her master's goods to the poor, and bore the early jealousy of the other servants with patience until her goodness won them over.

Many stories of her charity and of small marvels attending it spread through Lucca, and she was venerated as a saint immediately upon her death in 1272. Her cult was confirmed in 1696, and she is honoured as the patron of domestic workers and servants.
saints.knownFor: Sanctifying humble domestic service through charity and prayer.

canonization.canonized: Cult confirmed 1696 by Pope Innocent XII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 April

saints.name: St. Louis Marie de Montfort
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A tireless missionary of the poor whose “True Devotion” shaped modern Marian piety…
biography: Louis-Marie Grignion was born in 1673 at Montfort in Brittany. Ordained a priest, he gave himself to preaching parish missions among the poor of western France, walking from village to village, reviving faith through catechism, the Rosary, and dramatic renewals of baptismal promises, often meeting hostility from those he challenged.

He founded the Company of Mary and the Daughters of Wisdom to continue his work. His writings, above all the Treatise on True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin, taught total consecration to Christ through Mary and profoundly influenced later Catholic devotion. Worn out by his labours, he died in 1716; he was beatified in 1888 and canonized in 1947.
saints.knownFor: His missions to the poor and his teaching on consecration to Christ through Mary.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Blessed Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 April

saints.name: St. Catherine of Siena
saints.title: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Dominican mystic of Siena whose letters and Dialogue moved popes, and who helped bring the papacy home from Avignon…
biography: The youngest of many children of a Sienese dyer, Catherine took the Dominican habit as a laywoman and gave herself to prayer and to the service of the sick and poor. Her mystical graces and her fearless letters drew disciples and won her a hearing among princes and prelates; she is credited with persuading Pope Gregory XI to return from Avignon to Rome.
She dictated her Dialogue of Divine Providence and died at thirty-three in Rome, worn out by her labors for the Church. She was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1970 and a patron of Europe.
saints.knownFor: Recalling the popes to Rome and her mystical writings.

canonization.canonized: 1461 by Pope Pius II; Doctor of the Church (1970)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 April

saints.name: Pope St. Pius V
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The Dominican pope who carried out the reforms of Trent and gave the Church the feast of the Rosary…
biography: Antonio Ghislieri, born in 1504 near Alessandria, entered the Dominicans as a boy, rose through the Roman Inquisition, and was elected pope in 1566, taking the name Pius V. Austere and single-minded, he lived as a friar in the papal palace and made it his life's work to enforce the reforms of the Council of Trent.

He issued the Roman Catechism, reformed the Breviary, and promulgated the renewed Roman Missal that shaped the Latin Mass for four centuries. In 1571 he forged the Holy League whose fleet turned back the Ottoman navy at Lepanto, a victory he attributed to the Rosary and commemorated in the feast now kept as Our Lady of the Rosary. He died in 1572 and was canonized in 1712.
saints.knownFor: Enforcing the Council of Trent and the victory of Lepanto.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 April

saints.name: St. Joseph the Worker
saints.title: Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The carpenter of Nazareth, guardian of the Holy Family, whose daily labor sanctifies all honest work…
biography: St. Joseph, a descendant of David, was the husband of the Virgin Mary and the foster-father of Jesus. The Gospels call him a “just man” (Matthew 1:19) and a carpenter (tekton), and it was in his workshop at Nazareth that the Son of God was reared and learned a trade. He is not recorded as speaking a single word in Scripture, yet he obeyed each command of the angel without hesitation.

In 1955 Pope Pius XII instituted the memorial of St. Joseph the Worker for the first of May, setting the dignity of Christian labor over against the secular observances of that day. Long honored as patron of the universal Church, Joseph is held up as the model of the working man who offers his toil to God.
saints.knownFor: The dignity of human labor, sanctified in the carpenter of Nazareth.

saints.name: St. Athanasius
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The unbending bishop of Alexandria who stood “against the world” for the divinity of Christ through five exiles…
biography: Athanasius attended the Council of Nicaea as a young deacon and became bishop of Alexandria soon after. For nearly half a century he defended the Nicene doctrine that the Son is of one being with the Father, suffering five exiles at the hands of Arian emperors — whence the saying, Athanasius contra mundum, “Athanasius against the world.”
He wrote the classic Life of St. Antony, which spread monasticism across the West. He is honored as a Doctor of the Church.
saints.knownFor: His lifelong defense of Christ's divinity against Arianism.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 2 May

saints.name: Sts. Philip and James
saints.title: Apostles
saints.shortBlurb: Two of the Twelve, joined in a single feast because their relics were together enshrined at Rome…
biography: Philip, a native of Bethsaida in Galilee, was among the first called by Jesus and appears several times in the Gospel of John, once asking, “Lord, show us the Father” (John 14:8). Tradition holds that he preached in Phrygia and died at Hierapolis. James, called “the Less” to distinguish him from the son of Zebedee, was the son of Alphaeus and, by long tradition, the first bishop of Jerusalem and author of the epistle bearing his name.

The two apostles are celebrated together because the dedication of the Roman basilica of the Holy Apostles, where their relics were placed, fell on this day. Both are honored as martyrs who gave their lives for the Gospel.
saints.knownFor: Their apostolic witness to Christ, sealed in martyrdom.

saints.name: St. Florian
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman officer in Noricum who confessed Christ and was drowned in the Enns during Diocletian's persecution…
biography: Florian was a senior officer in the Roman army stationed in the province of Noricum, in what is now Austria. When the persecution of Diocletian broke out, he openly professed his faith and gave himself up rather than deny Christ, encouraging imprisoned Christians at the town of Lorch.

He was condemned, scourged, and, with a millstone tied about his neck, drowned in the river Enns about the year 304. His relics were greatly venerated, and he became one of the principal patrons of Poland and Upper Austria; because he was invoked against fire and flood, he is honored as the patron of firefighters.
saints.knownFor: His steadfast confession under Diocletian and his patronage of firefighters.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Hilary of Arles
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A monk of Lérins raised young to the see of Arles, austere in life and famed for his eloquence…
biography: Hilary was drawn to the monastery of Lérins under the influence of his kinsman St. Honoratus, whom he followed to Arles when Honoratus became bishop there. On the death of Honoratus about 429 the still-young Hilary was chosen to succeed him.

As bishop he lived with great austerity, worked with his own hands to relieve the poor, and preached with such power that he was reckoned among the finest orators of Gaul. A dispute over his exercise of authority beyond his province brought him into conflict with Pope St. Leo the Great, yet Leo praised his holiness. He died at Arles in 449.
saints.knownFor: His ascetic zeal and eloquent preaching as Bishop of Arles.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 May

saints.name: St. Dominic Savio
saints.title: Youth
saints.shortBlurb: A boy of the Oratory under St. John Bosco who resolved to “die rather than sin,” dead before his fifteenth year…
biography: Born to a peasant family near Turin in 1842, Dominic Savio came under the care of St. John Bosco, who received him into his Oratory. There the boy pursued holiness with an ardor beyond his years, taking as his motto, “Death rather than sin,” and gathering companions into a sodality devoted to Our Lady.

His health, never strong, failed him, and he died at home on 9 March 1857, not yet fifteen, saying he saw “something wonderful.” John Bosco wrote his life, and the Church later held him up as a model of youthful sanctity; the Salesian family keeps his memory on this day.
saints.knownFor: Youthful holiness formed under St. John Bosco.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Dominic Savio (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. John of Beverley
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Northumbrian bishop and teacher who ordained the Venerable Bede and ended his days in the monastery he founded…
biography: John was educated at the abbey of Whitby under St. Hilda and became bishop first of Hexham and then of York. Renowned for learning and charity, he ordained the young Bede both deacon and priest; Bede in turn recorded the miracles and holiness of his teacher.
In old age John withdrew to the monastery he had founded at Beverley, where he died in 721. His tomb became a center of pilgrimage, and he was formally canonized in 1037.
saints.knownFor: His holy episcopate and the ordination of the Venerable Bede.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 May

saints.name: St. Peter of Tarentaise
saints.title: Archbishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Cistercian monk drawn from his cloister to govern the see of Tarentaise, beloved for his boundless charity…
biography: Peter entered the Cistercian order and became abbot of Tabennes before he was, against his will, made Archbishop of Tarentaise in the Alps about 1142. He reformed his diocese, founded hospices for travelers in the mountain passes, and instituted a distribution of bread to the poor that continued long after his death.

So heavy did the burden of office weigh on him that he once fled his see to live hidden as a lay brother, until he was discovered and brought back. He labored to heal the papal schism of his day and died in 1174 while on such a mission; he was canonized in 1191.
saints.knownFor: His Cistercian sanctity and charity as Archbishop of Tarentaise.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 May

saints.name: St. Pachomius
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The Egyptian soldier-turned-hermit who gathered the desert solitaries into community and wrote monasticism's first Rule…
biography: Born in the Thebaid of Egypt about 292, Pachomius was conscripted into the Roman army, where the kindness of Christians won him to the faith. After his baptism he withdrew into the desert as a hermit under the guidance of the aged Palemon.

About the year 320 at Tabennisi he began to gather solitaries into an ordered community, or cenobium, and drew up a written Rule governing prayer, work, and common life — the first of its kind. By his death in 348 thousands of monks and nuns lived under his direction, and his Rule shaped monasticism throughout the Church.
saints.knownFor: Founding cenobitic (communal) monasticism and its first written Rule.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Damien of Molokai
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Belgian missionary who gave his life to the abandoned lepers of Molokai and died one of them…
biography: Jozef De Veuster was born in Belgium in 1840 and took the name Damien on entering the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts. Sent to the Hawaiian Islands, he volunteered in 1873 to serve the leper colony at Kalaupapa on Molokai, where the sick had been exiled without adequate care.

For sixteen years he built homes, churches, and coffins, dressed wounds, and shared every hardship of his people, until he too contracted the disease. He famously began a sermon, “We lepers…,” and died among them in 1889. He was canonized in 2009 and is honored in the United States on this day.
saints.knownFor: A life laid down for the lepers of Molokai.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Damien de Veuster (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Mamertus
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Bishop of Vienne in Gaul who instituted the Rogation Days of penitential prayer and procession…
biography: Mamertus was Archbishop of Vienne in southern Gaul in the fifth century, a time of earthquakes, fires, and other calamities that struck his region. To turn away these afflictions he appointed three days of fasting, litanies, and processions before the feast of the Ascension.
This observance, the Rogation Days, spread throughout the Western Church and endured for many centuries. He died about 475, remembered chiefly as the author of these public prayers.
saints.knownFor: Instituting the Rogation Days of prayer and procession.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 May

saints.name: St. Pancras
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A boy of about fourteen who was beheaded at Rome rather than sacrifice to the gods…
biography: According to his ancient acts, Pancras was born in Phrygia and brought as an orphan to Rome, where he was converted to Christianity. During the persecution of Diocletian he refused to offer sacrifice and was beheaded on the Aurelian Way, still only a boy of about fourteen.

His tomb became one of the great pilgrim shrines of Rome, and his name spread widely; a Roman church and, later, the London district and railway station of St. Pancras bear his name. He is often joined in the Roman calendar with the martyrs Nereus and Achilleus, kept the same day.
saints.knownFor: His youthful martyrdom at Rome under Diocletian.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Our Lady of Fatima
saints.title: Marian Memorial
saints.shortBlurb: The 1917 apparitions of the Virgin Mary to three shepherd children at Fatima, calling the world to prayer and penance…
biography: On 13 May 1917, near the Portuguese village of Fatima, three shepherd children — Lúcia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto — reported the first of six apparitions of a Lady “brighter than the sun.” Through them she asked for the daily Rosary, prayer, and penance for the conversion of sinners and the peace of the world.

The apparitions culminated on 13 October, when a crowd of thousands witnessed what became known as the Miracle of the Sun. Francisco and Jacinta died young and were canonized in 2017; the message of Fatima has remained among the most influential of modern Marian devotions.
saints.knownFor: The call to prayer, penance, and the Rosary given at Fatima in 1917.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Shepherds of Fatima (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Matthias
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: Chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve, a witness to the Lord from His baptism to the Ascension…
biography: After the Ascension, the eleven Apostles, needing to fill the place left by Judas, put forward two who had followed Jesus from the beginning; having prayed, they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Matthias, who was numbered with the Twelve. Of his later labors little is known with certainty; tradition sends him to preach in Judea and beyond.
He is honored as an Apostle and a martyr.
saints.knownFor: Completing the Twelve after the Ascension.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 February

saints.name: St. Isidore the Farmer
saints.title: Layman
saints.shortBlurb: A day-laborer of Madrid who sanctified the plough and the field with unceasing prayer…
biography: Isidore was born of poor parents near Madrid about 1070 and spent his whole life as a hired hand working the fields of a wealthy landowner. He rose early for Mass before his labor, and pious legend tells of angels guiding his plough while he prayed. With his wife, St. Maria de la Cabeza, he shared his bread with the poor and the beasts alike.

He died in 1130 and was long venerated in Spain before being canonized in 1622 in the same ceremony as Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, and Philip Neri. In the United States he is honored as patron of farmers and rural life.
saints.knownFor: Sanctity found in the daily labor of the fields.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 May

saints.name: St. John Nepomucene
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The priest of Prague who was drowned in the Vltava, remembered as a martyr of the seal of confession…
biography: John was born at Nepomuk in Bohemia and became vicar-general of the Archbishop of Prague. He fell into conflict with King Wenceslaus IV over the rights of the Church, and in 1393 he was tortured and cast, bound, from a bridge into the river Vltava.

Long tradition holds that the king's anger was inflamed because John, as confessor to the queen, refused to reveal what she had confided under the seal of confession. For this reason he has been venerated for centuries as the patron of confessors and of those unjustly accused, and his statues stand upon bridges throughout central Europe.
saints.knownFor: Dying rather than betray the seal of confession.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 May

saints.name: St. Paschal Baylon
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A Spanish shepherd-boy turned Franciscan lay brother, burning with love for the Blessed Sacrament…
biography: Born to peasant parents in Aragon in 1540, Paschal tended sheep in his youth and taught himself to read from a borrowed book so that he might follow the Mass. At about twenty-four he entered the Franciscans as a lay brother, serving as porter, cook, and doorkeeper with unfailing humility.

His whole life was marked by an intense devotion to the Eucharist, before which he would kneel for hours. He died at Villareal in 1592, reputedly at the moment of the elevation at Mass, and was canonized in 1690; Pope Leo XIII later named him patron of Eucharistic congresses and confraternities.
saints.knownFor: His ardent devotion to the Blessed Sacrament.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 17 May

saints.name: Pope St. John I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A pope sent unwillingly on an embassy by an Arian king, who died a prisoner on his return…
biography: A native of Tuscany, John was elected to the See of Peter in 523. The Ostrogothic king Theodoric, an Arian, compelled him to lead an embassy to the Emperor Justin at Constantinople on behalf of the Arians of the East — the first pope to travel to the imperial city.

There he was received with the highest honor and is said to have crowned the emperor, but on his return Theodoric, suspicious of his loyalty, had him imprisoned at Ravenna, where he died of ill treatment in 526. He has been honored ever since as a martyr.
saints.knownFor: His witness unto death amid the Arian conflict.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Dunstan
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Abbot of Glastonbury and Archbishop of Canterbury who revived English monastic life in the tenth century…
biography: Dunstan was born near Glastonbury and rose to be its abbot, where he restored monastic discipline according to the Rule of St. Benedict. A statesman as well as a monk, he served several kings of the English and was made Archbishop of Canterbury about 960.

With the bishops Ethelwold and Oswald he led a great reform of the English Church, founding and renewing monasteries throughout the land. Skilled as a metalworker, scribe, and musician, he is remembered as patron of goldsmiths; he died at Canterbury in 988.
saints.knownFor: The revival of English monastic life as Archbishop of Canterbury.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 19 May

saints.name: St. Bernardine of Siena
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Franciscan preacher who carried the Holy Name of Jesus across Italy on his famous tablet…
biography: Bernardine was born of a noble Sienese family in 1380 and, orphaned young, gave himself to works of mercy before entering the Franciscans. He became the most celebrated preacher of his age, traveling on foot across Italy and drawing enormous crowds with his plain, vivid sermons against usury, faction, and vice.

He spread devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus, displaying to his hearers a tablet bearing the monogram IHS radiant with gold. Three times he refused a bishopric that he might continue to preach, and he labored to reform his order. He died at Aquila in 1444 and was canonized only six years later.
saints.knownFor: Preaching the Holy Name of Jesus across Italy.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 20 May

saints.name: St. Christopher Magallanes and Companions
saints.title: Priests and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A Mexican parish priest and his fellow martyrs, killed in the persecution of the Church during the Cristero years…
biography: Cristóbal Magallanes Jara was born in Jalisco, Mexico, in 1869 and became a parish priest at Totatiche, where he founded a seminary when the government closed the official ones. During the anticlerical persecution that followed the Mexican revolution, the public exercise of the faith was outlawed and many priests were hunted down.

Arrested while on his way to say Mass, Magallanes was shot without trial in 1927, absolving his executioners and declaring his innocence. He is honored together with twenty-four companions — priests and laymen martyred between 1915 and 1937 — canonized in 2000.
saints.knownFor: Faithful priests martyred in Mexico's persecution of the Church.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Cristóbal Magallanes and Companions (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Rita of Cascia
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: The wife, mother, and widow who became an Augustinian nun, honored as the saint of impossible causes…
biography: Born near Cascia in Umbria about 1381, Rita was given in marriage young to a harsh husband; she bore his ill temper with patience and, after his violent death, forgave his killers and prevented her sons from taking revenge. Widowed and then bereft of both sons, she sought entry to the Augustinian convent at Cascia and was at last admitted.

For forty years she lived in prayer and penance, receiving, it is said, a wound on her forehead as though from a thorn of Christ's crown. She died in 1457, and popular devotion made her the advocate of desperate and seemingly hopeless situations; she was canonized in 1900.
saints.knownFor: Patient endurance and intercession in impossible causes.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 May

saints.name: St. John Baptist de Rossi
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman priest who gave himself wholly to the poor, the sick, and the outcasts of the city…
biography: Born in Liguria in 1698, John Baptist de Rossi came to Rome as a boy and was ordained despite recurring epilepsy that at times prevented him from preaching. He devoted himself to the neglected of the city — carters, herdsmen, the homeless, and prisoners — and to the women in the public hospice whom others would not approach.
He became one of the most sought-after confessors in Rome, hearing penitents for long hours, and refused honors that he might continue his humble ministry. He died in 1764 and was canonized in 1881.
saints.knownFor: His tireless ministry to Rome's poor and in the confessional.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John Baptist de Rossi”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 May

saints.name: St. Vincent of Lérins
saints.title: Monk
saints.shortBlurb: The monk of Lérins who gave the Church its enduring test of authentic tradition…
biography: Vincent was a monk of the island monastery of Lérins off the coast of Gaul in the first half of the fifth century. Under the pen-name Peregrinus he wrote the Commonitorium, a short treatise on how to distinguish true Catholic doctrine from heresy.

There he set down his famous rule: that we hold to what has been believed “everywhere, always, and by all” (quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus). This “Vincentian Canon” has guided theologians ever since. He died about 445.
saints.knownFor: The rule for discerning authentic Catholic teaching — held everywhere, always, by all.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 May

saints.name: St. Bede the Venerable
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The monk of Jarrow whose history first told the story of the English Church, the “Father of English History”…
biography: Given as a boy to the monastery of Wearmouth-Jarrow in Northumbria, Bede spent his whole life there in study, teaching, and prayer. From that small cloister he produced commentaries on Scripture, works on chronology and computation, and above all the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, the chief source for the early Christian history of England.

He completed his last work, a translation of the Gospel of John, on the very day he died in 735, dictating its final words to a scribe. Honored as “Venerable” from soon after his death, he was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1899, the only Englishman so named.
saints.knownFor: His Ecclesiastical History of the English People.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1899)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 May

saints.name: St. Philip Neri
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The joyful “Apostle of Rome” and founder of the Oratory, who won souls through cheerfulness and charity…
biography: Born in Florence in 1515, Philip came to Rome as a young man and spent years in prayer and quiet service before his ordination in 1551. He drew about him disciples for informal gatherings of prayer, Scripture, and sacred music, out of which grew the Congregation of the Oratory.

Famous for his humor, humility, and warmth, he steered penitents to holiness by gentleness rather than severity and became so beloved a figure that he was called the “Apostle of Rome.” He died in 1595 and was canonized in 1622 alongside Ignatius, Xavier, Teresa, and Isidore.
saints.knownFor: The joyful Apostle of Rome and founder of the Oratory.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 26 May

saints.name: St. Augustine of Canterbury
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Roman monk sent by Pope Gregory the Great to convert the English, and first Archbishop of Canterbury…
biography: Augustine was prior of St. Andrew's monastery in Rome when Pope St. Gregory the Great sent him and a band of monks to evangelize the Anglo-Saxons. Landing in Kent in 597, he was received by King Ethelbert, whose Christian wife Bertha aided the mission; the king was soon baptized, and thousands followed.

Consecrated bishop, Augustine established his see at Canterbury and founded churches and a monastery there. Though his efforts to unite the ancient British Christians with Rome met resistance, he laid the foundation of the English Church and is honored as the “Apostle of the English.” He died about 604.
saints.knownFor: The conversion of the English and the founding of the see of Canterbury.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 26 May

saints.name: St. Bernard of Menthon
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The archdeacon of Aosta who built the Alpine hospices that sheltered travelers for a thousand years…
biography: Bernard served as archdeacon of Aosta in the western Alps, where his chief work was among the poor and among the pilgrims and merchants crossing the dangerous mountain passes toward Rome. Robbers and the perils of snow and cold claimed many lives on those heights.

To protect travelers he founded hospices at the two passes that still bear his name, the Great and Little St. Bernard, entrusting them to communities of canons whose rescue-dogs later became famous. He died about 1008; in 1923 Pope Pius XI named him the patron of mountaineers and Alpinists.
saints.knownFor: The Alpine hospices that sheltered travelers for centuries.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; named patron of Alpinists in 1923 by Pope Pius XI

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 May

saints.name: St. Paul VI
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who carried the Second Vatican Council to its close and steered the Church through its reforms…
biography: Giovanni Battista Montini was born near Brescia in 1897 and served for decades in the papal secretariat of state before becoming Archbishop of Milan and, in 1963, Pope Paul VI. He guided the remaining sessions of the Second Vatican Council to their conclusion and oversaw the implementation of its decrees.

He was the first pope in modern times to travel abroad widely — to the Holy Land, to the United Nations, and to every continent — and in 1968 issued the encyclical Humanae Vitae. He died in 1978 and was canonized in 2018.
saints.knownFor: Guiding the Church through the close of the Second Vatican Council.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Paul VI (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Joan of Arc
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The peasant girl who, led by heavenly voices, lifted the siege of Orléans and died at the stake at nineteen…
biography: Born about 1412 at Domrémy in Lorraine, Joan was an unlettered peasant girl who, from the age of thirteen, said she heard the voices of Sts. Michael, Catherine, and Margaret bidding her save France. In 1429 she persuaded the dauphin Charles to give her troops, relieved the besieged city of Orléans, and saw him crowned king at Reims.

Captured by the Burgundians and sold to the English, she was tried by an ecclesiastical court hostile to her cause and burned as a heretic at Rouen on 30 May 1431, calling on the name of Jesus. A later inquiry declared her innocent; she was canonized in 1920 and is a patron of France.
saints.knownFor: The Maid of Orléans who freed France and died at the stake.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 May

saints.name: The Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: Mary's journey to her cousin Elizabeth, where the unborn John leapt for joy and the Magnificat was sung…
biography: After the Annunciation, Mary went in haste into the hill country of Judea to visit her kinswoman Elizabeth, who had conceived John the Baptist in her old age. When Mary greeted her, the child leapt in Elizabeth's womb, and she cried out, “Blessed art thou among women” (Luke 1:39–45).

Mary answered with the Magnificat, her great hymn of praise: “My soul doth magnify the Lord.” The feast, kept on the last day of May in the reformed calendar, falls fittingly between the Annunciation and the Nativity of John the Baptist.
saints.knownFor: Mary's visit to Elizabeth and the song of the Magnificat.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary”

saints.name: St. Justin Martyr
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A philosopher who found in Christ the true wisdom he had long sought, and sealed his teaching with his blood…
biography: Born of pagan parents at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria about the year 100, Justin studied the schools of Greek philosophy until an encounter with an old man by the sea led him to the Scriptures and to faith in Christ. He continued to wear the philosopher's cloak, teaching the Gospel as the one sure philosophy, and opened a school at Rome.

His First and Second Apologies, addressed to the emperor, and his Dialogue with Trypho the Jew are among the earliest and most valuable defenses of the faith. Denounced as a Christian, he was scourged and beheaded at Rome about 165 under the prefect Rusticus, together with several companions.
saints.knownFor: His Apologies defending the faith to the pagan world.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Sts. Marcellinus and Peter
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman priest and an exorcist who died together under Diocletian and are still named in the Canon of the Mass…
biography: Marcellinus, a priest, and Peter, an exorcist, were among the most celebrated martyrs of the Roman Church, put to death in the persecution of Diocletian about the year 304. According to the epitaph composed by Pope St. Damasus, who as a boy had heard the account from their executioner, they were beheaded in a hidden place and buried on the Via Labicana.

The Emperor Constantine built a basilica over their tomb, near which his mother, St. Helena, was laid to rest. Their names were placed in the Canon of the Mass, where they are still invoked among the martyrs.
saints.knownFor: Their witness under Diocletian; named in the Roman Canon.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Charles Lwanga and Companions
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The young royal pages of Buganda who chose death by fire rather than betray their baptism…
biography: Charles Lwanga was master of the pages at the court of King Mwanga II of Buganda, in present-day Uganda. When the king, enraged at the Christian faith of his servants and at their refusal to submit to his abuses, turned to persecution, Charles and his companions — some newly baptized — held firm.

On 3 June 1886 Charles Lwanga and a number of the pages were bound and burned alive at Namugongo; others were put to death over the months of persecution, and Charles baptized several of the boys in secret before their deaths. Twenty-two of the Catholic martyrs were canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1964, the first canonized martyrs of modern Africa.
saints.knownFor: The first canonized martyrs of sub-Saharan Africa.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Charles Lwanga and Companions (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Francis Caracciolo
saints.title: Priest and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: An Italian nobleman who founded a religious order devoted above all to the Blessed Sacrament…
biography: Born Ascanio Caracciolo in the Abruzzi in 1563, he took the name Francis on joining a confraternity that ministered to prisoners condemned to death. With John Augustine Adorno he founded at Naples in 1588 the Clerks Regular Minor, who added to the usual vows a promise not to seek ecclesiastical office and gave themselves to perpetual adoration of the Eucharist.

Renowned for penance and for his love of the Blessed Sacrament, before which he spent long hours, he governed and spread his order until his death at Agnone in 1608. He was canonized by Pope Pius VII in 1807.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Clerks Regular Minor and Eucharistic devotion.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Boniface
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The English monk who became the apostle of Germany, felled the sacred oak of Thor, and died a martyr in Frisia…
biography: Born Winfrid in Wessex, Boniface left the cloister to evangelize the Germanic peoples under commission from Rome. He is remembered for felling the great Oak of Thor at Geismar, which won many to the faith, and for organizing the Church across Germany, founding sees and the abbey of Fulda.
An old man, still a missionary, he was slain with his companions by pagans in Frisia while awaiting a group of converts for confirmation.
saints.knownFor: Evangelizing and organizing the Church in Germany.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 June

saints.name: St. Norbert
saints.title: Bishop and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A worldly cleric converted by a brush with death, who became a great preacher and founded the Premonstratensians…
biography: Born at Xanten in the Rhineland about 1080, Norbert lived an easy life as a courtier-cleric until, thrown from his horse in a storm, he took the near-fatal shock as a summons to conversion. Ordained and giving away his goods, he became a wandering preacher of penance and, in 1120, founded a community of canons at Prémontré who followed the Rule of St. Augustine — the Premonstratensians, or Norbertines.

Called against his will to be Archbishop of Magdeburg, he labored to reform the clergy and was a strong defender of belief in the Real Presence against the errors of Tanchelm. He died at Magdeburg in 1134 and was canonized in 1582.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Premonstratensian canons; devotion to the Eucharist.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 June

saints.name: St. Robert of Newminster
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: An English Cistercian abbot of gentle rule and great austerity, friend of the hermit St. Godric…
biography: Born at Gargrave in Yorkshire about 1100, Robert became a parish priest and then a monk, joining the reforming movement that produced the great Cistercian houses of the north of England. He was among the founders of Newminster Abbey in Northumberland in 1138 and served as its first abbot, from which other monasteries were in turn established.
Noted for his austerity, gentleness, and gift of prayer, he was a friend of the hermit St. Godric of Finchale. He died at Newminster in 1159.
saints.knownFor: First abbot of Newminster; Cistercian holiness.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 June
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Medard
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: One of the most beloved bishops of ancient Gaul, remembered for his charity and long woven into French folklore…
biography: Medard was born at Salency in Picardy about the year 456 and became Bishop of Vermand, moving the see to the safer town of Noyon amid the disorders of the age. Famed for his charity and zeal, he is counted among the most honored of the early bishops of France.

He is said to have given the veil to St. Radegund and by tradition founded the festival of the Rosière at Salency, at which a virtuous maiden was crowned each year. He died about 545, and popular weather-lore in France still attaches to his feast.
saints.knownFor: His charity as a bishop of ancient Gaul.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 June

saints.name: St. Ephrem the Syrian
saints.title: Deacon and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The “Harp of the Holy Spirit,” whose hymns taught the faith and adorned the worship of the Syriac Church…
biography: Born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia about 306, Ephrem served the Church there and, after the city passed to Persia, at Edessa, where he taught in the famous school and lived as a deacon and ascetic. He wrote a vast body of hymns, homilies, and commentaries in Syriac, defending orthodoxy against the heresies of his day.

So celebrated were his hymns, sung by choirs in the churches, that he was called the “Harp of the Holy Spirit.” He died at Edessa in 373 while ministering to victims of famine, and in 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the Church.
saints.knownFor: His hymns and the title “Harp of the Holy Spirit.”

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; declared a Doctor of the Church in 1920

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Landericus of Paris
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Paris who founded the city's first hospital out of love for the poor…
biography: Landericus, known in French as Landry, was Bishop of Paris in the middle of the seventh century. Moved by the sufferings of the poor during a time of famine, he sold his goods and even sacred vessels to feed them.
He is remembered above all as the founder of the Hôtel-Dieu, the great hospital of Paris that endured for centuries as a house of charity. He died about the year 660.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Hôtel-Dieu, the first hospital of Paris.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 10 June
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Barnabas
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: The “son of encouragement,” a Levite of Cyprus who vouched for Paul and carried the Gospel to the Gentiles…
biography: Barnabas, a Levite of Cyprus, sold his land for the early community and was the one who brought the newly converted Paul to the Apostles when others feared him. Sent to Antioch, he fetched Paul to help him, and the two were set apart for the first missionary journey; though not one of the Twelve, he is called an Apostle.
Tradition holds that he preached in Cyprus and was there martyred.
saints.knownFor: Encouraging the young Church and befriending St. Paul.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 June

saints.name: St. John of Sahagún
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: An Augustinian friar and fearless preacher who made peace in the feuding city of Salamanca…
biography: Born at Sahagún in the kingdom of León about 1419, John studied and was ordained, then entered the Hermits of St. Augustine at Salamanca in 1463. He became the most powerful preacher of that university city, rebuking vice without fear of the great.

His frank preaching quelled the bloody feuds of the noble factions of Salamanca, of which he is honored as patron. Devoted to the Eucharist, he died in 1479 — some said poisoned by those his words had rebuked — and was canonized in 1690.
saints.knownFor: Preaching peace to feuding Salamanca.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 12 June

saints.name: St. Anthony of Padua
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Portuguese Franciscan of dazzling preaching and learning, invoked the world over for the finding of what is lost…
biography: Born at Lisbon, Anthony first joined the Augustinians but, drawn by the martyrdom of Franciscan friars, took the habit of St. Francis. His profound knowledge of Scripture and his eloquence made him a renowned preacher across Italy and France, and the first teacher of theology in the Order.
He died young at Padua in 1231 and was canonized within the year. He is a Doctor of the Church and is popularly invoked to recover lost things.
saints.knownFor: His preaching and learning; patron of lost things.

canonization.canonized: 1232 by Pope Gregory IX; Doctor of the Church (1946)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 June

saints.name: St. Methodius I of Constantinople
saints.title: Patriarch
saints.shortBlurb: The patriarch who saw the final restoration of the holy images after long years of iconoclasm…
biography: A native of Syracuse in Sicily, Methodius went to Constantinople and became a monk, entering the long struggle over the veneration of sacred images. For his defense of the icons he suffered imprisonment and harsh confinement under the iconoclast emperors.

Raised to the patriarchal throne in 843 under the Empress Theodora, he presided over the definitive restoration of the images — the event celebrated in the East as the “Triumph of Orthodoxy.” He governed the Church of Constantinople until his death in 847.
saints.knownFor: The restoration of sacred images in 843.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Vitus
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A boy martyr of the early Church, one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers invoked in sickness…
biography: According to his ancient acts, Vitus was the young son of a pagan senator in Sicily who was converted as a child by his tutor Modestus and his nurse Crescentia. Fleeing his father's anger, the three were seized in the persecution of Diocletian and put to death about the year 303.

His veneration spread widely through the West, and he came to be numbered among the Fourteen Holy Helpers. He is invoked against epilepsy and the nervous disorder long called “St. Vitus's Dance,” and is honored as a patron of dancers and actors.
saints.knownFor: One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers; patron of dancers.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. John Francis Regis
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A tireless Jesuit missionary of the French mountains, apostle of the poor and of the forsaken…
biography: Born in Languedoc in 1597, John Francis Regis entered the Society of Jesus and gave himself to missions among the neglected people of the mountainous Vivarais and Velay. In summer he catechized in the towns and in winter tramped through snow to remote villages, reconciling sinners and reviving the faith.

He founded confraternities to care for the poor and to rescue women from prostitution, enduring opposition for it. Worn out and caught in a winter storm, he died at Lalouvesc at the close of 1640, and was canonized in 1737.
saints.knownFor: His missions among the poor of the French highlands.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Botulph
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: An English abbot whose name lives on in the town of Boston, “Botolph's town”…
biography: Botulph (or Botolph) was a seventh-century English monk who, about the year 654, founded a monastery at Icanho in East Anglia, generally identified with Iken in Suffolk. He was esteemed for his learning and holiness and drew disciples to the monastic life.
Many ancient churches in England were dedicated to him, especially at town gates, for he was invoked as a patron of travelers. The town of Boston takes its very name from “Botolph's town.”
saints.knownFor: Founding the abbey of Icanho; patron of travelers.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 17 June
The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Sts. Mark and Marcellian
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Twin brothers of Rome strengthened in their last trial by the encouragement of St. Sebastian…
biography: Mark and Marcellian were twin brothers of a distinguished Roman family, converted to Christ and arrested in the persecution of Diocletian about the year 286. Wavering under the pleadings of their pagan parents, they were, according to their acts, confirmed in constancy by the exhortations of St. Sebastian.
Refusing to sacrifice to the gods, they were bound and put to death, and were buried on the Via Ardeatina. Their memory was long kept in the Roman Church.
saints.knownFor: Their steadfast martyrdom at Rome.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Romuald
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: A nobleman of Ravenna who became a hermit and founded the Camaldolese, wedding the monastic and eremitic life…
biography: Born about 951 to a noble family of Ravenna, Romuald fled the world after witnessing his father kill a kinsman in a duel, doing penance in a Benedictine monastery. Drawn to the solitary life, he spent years as a hermit and reformer, traveling widely to restore fervor to monasteries and to guide would-be martyrs.
About 1023 he established at Camaldoli in the Apennines a community that joined the life of hermits with that of monks — the Camaldolese Benedictines. He died in solitude at Val di Castro in 1027.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Camaldolese Benedictines.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Pope St. Silverius
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A pope deposed and exiled for refusing to restore a heretic, who died in banishment for the faith…
biography: Silverius, son of Pope Hormisdas, was raised to the See of Peter in 536 amid the wars of Justinian's reconquest of Italy. When the Empress Theodora pressed him to reinstate the deposed Monophysite patriarch Anthimus of Constantinople, he refused.

For this he was falsely accused, stripped of the papacy, and banished by the general Belisarius; he was exiled to the island of Palmaria, where he died of privation in 537. The Church has long honored him as a martyr.
saints.knownFor: Suffering exile rather than betray the faith.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Aloysius Gonzaga
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A young prince who renounced a marquisate for the Society of Jesus and died nursing the plague-stricken…
biography: Born in 1568 heir to the marquisate of Castiglione in Lombardy, Aloysius was raised for a soldier's and courtier's life but resolved from boyhood on purity and prayer. Renouncing his inheritance in favor of his brother, he entered the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1585 and studied under St. Robert Bellarmine.

When plague struck Rome in 1591, he gave himself to nursing the sick in the Jesuits' hospital, caught the contagion, and died at the age of twenty-three. He was canonized in 1726 and is honored as a patron of youth and of students.
saints.knownFor: His purity and self-sacrifice; patron of youth.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 June

saints.name: St. Paulinus of Nola
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman senator and poet who gave away his wealth to serve Christ and the tomb of St. Felix…
biography: Born about 354 at Bordeaux to a wealthy senatorial family, Pontius Meropius Paulinus held high office before he and his wife Therasia, moved by grace, renounced their vast estates and embraced a life of poverty and prayer. He settled at Nola in Campania near the tomb of St. Felix, whom he honored each year in verse.

Chosen bishop of Nola, he was renowned for his charity and for his friendships with Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and Sulpicius Severus, with whom he kept up a rich correspondence. A Christian poet of note, he died in 431.
saints.knownFor: His poetry and his renunciation of wealth for Christ.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 June

saints.name: St. Etheldreda
saints.title: Abbess
saints.shortBlurb: An East Anglian princess who kept her vow of virginity through two marriages and founded the abbey of Ely…
biography: Etheldreda (Audrey), daughter of King Anna of East Anglia, was married twice for reasons of state yet, by her own account, preserved her virginity throughout. At last released, she received the veil and about 673 founded a double monastery at Ely, over which she ruled as abbess in great austerity.
She died in 679, and her body was found incorrupt, making Ely a famed place of pilgrimage. From the trinkets once sold at her fair the English word “tawdry” — from “St. Audrey” — is derived.
saints.knownFor: Founding Ely Abbey; her consecrated virginity.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 23 June

saints.name: The Nativity of St. John the Baptist
saints.title: Precursor of the Lord
saints.shortBlurb: The forerunner sent to prepare the way of the Lord, whose birth to Zechariah and Elizabeth the Church keeps with joy…
biography: The birth of John, son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth in her old age, was foretold by the angel Gabriel; at his naming his father's speech returned, and he prophesied. John grew up in the desert and came preaching a baptism of repentance, pointing to Christ as the Lamb of God, and was beheaded by Herod.
His nativity, set six months before Christmas, is one of the few birthdays the Church celebrates, for he was sanctified in his mother's womb.
saints.knownFor: Preparing the way for Christ as His forerunner.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 June

saints.name: St. Prosper of Aquitaine
saints.title: Theologian
saints.shortBlurb: A learned layman who became the great defender of St. Augustine's teaching on grace…
biography: Born in Aquitaine about 390, Prosper was a well-educated layman who took up his pen in defense of St. Augustine's doctrine of grace against the semi-Pelagians of southern Gaul. He corresponded with Augustine himself and, after the saint's death, carried the dispute to Rome.

He is thought to have assisted Pope St. Leo the Great and compiled a chronicle of world history that is a valuable source for his age. A model of the learned and faithful layman, he died at Rome about 455.
saints.knownFor: Defending St. Augustine's teaching on grace.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: Sts. John and Paul
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two brothers of Rome, martyred under Julian the Apostate, whose names are spoken in the Canon of the Mass…
