biography: Matthew, also called Levi, was a publican — a collector of taxes at Capernaum — when Jesus passed by and said, “Follow me”; he rose at once and left all. He gave a feast for the Lord with his fellow tax-gatherers, drawing the murmur of the Pharisees and the Lord's word that He came to call sinners.
He is honored as the author of the first Gospel, written for Jewish Christians, and as a martyr; his symbol is a winged man.
saints.knownFor: Leaving his tax table to follow Christ; writing the first Gospel.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 21 September

saints.name: St. Maurice and the Theban Legion
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: A legion of Christian soldiers who, led by their commander Maurice, chose death rather than turn their swords against the innocent or deny their faith…
biography: According to ancient tradition, the Theban Legion was a body of Christian soldiers recruited in Egypt and serving under the Emperor Maximian. Ordered, while stationed at Agaunum in the Alps, to take part in the persecution of Christians and to offer pagan sacrifice, they refused under their officer Maurice.

The legion was, it is said, twice decimated and at last put to the sword entire rather than yield. Over their reputed burial place rose the great abbey of Saint-Maurice in the Valais, one of the oldest continuously inhabited monasteries in the West.
saints.knownFor: Their refusal to persecute fellow Christians, sealed by martyrdom.

saints.name: St. Pius of Pietrelcina
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Capuchin friar known to the world as Padre Pio, who bore the wounds of Christ and spent his days in the confessional…
biography: Born Francesco Forgione at Pietrelcina in 1887, he took the Capuchin habit and the name Pio and was ordained a priest in 1910. From 1918 he bore the visible stigmata — the wounds of the crucified Christ — which he carried for half a century at the friary of San Giovanni Rotondo.

For decades he heard confessions many hours a day, drawing pilgrims from across the world, and founded a great hospital, the "Home for the Relief of Suffering." Investigated and for a time restricted by Church authorities, he bore it in obedience. He died in 1968 and was canonized by Pope John Paul II in 2002.
saints.knownFor: The stigmata he bore and his long ministry of confession and healing.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Pius of Pietrelcina (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Pacificus of San Severino
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Franciscan preacher of the Marches who, struck blind, deaf, and lame, turned his long affliction into a hidden life of prayer…
biography: Born at San Severino in the March of Ancona in 1653 and orphaned young, Pacificus entered the Franciscan Reformati and was ordained in 1678, labouring for some years as a missionary preacher among the country people. He then lost his hearing and sight and became lame, so that he could preach no longer.

For nearly thirty years he bore these infirmities with serene patience, giving himself instead to prayer, especially before the Blessed Sacrament, and to counsel of those who sought him. He died at San Severino in 1721, was beatified in 1786, and canonized by Pope Gregory XVI in 1839.
saints.knownFor: His patient endurance of affliction and his hidden life of prayer.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "St. Pacificus of San Severino"

saints.name: St. Finnbarr of Cork
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The hermit of the lake at Gougane Barra who founded the monastery and school from which the city of Cork arose…
biography: Finnbarr (Barra) was an early Irish monk and hermit who withdrew to a lonely island on a lake among the hills at the place now called Gougane Barra, the source of the river Lee. Disciples gathered to him, and he later moved downriver to found a monastery and school on the marshy ground where the city of Cork afterward grew.
Honoured as first bishop and patron of Cork, he was renowned for his learning and his monks, and died about 623. His cult has been kept in the south of Ireland from ancient times.
saints.knownFor: Founding the monastery and school that became the city of Cork.

saints.name: Sts. Cosmas and Damian
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Twin physicians who healed the sick without payment for the love of Christ, and were crowned with martyrdom…
biography: Cosmas and Damian, held by tradition to be twin brothers of Arabia, practised medicine in Syria and would take no fee for their care of the sick, so that they were called the "moneyless ones." Their charity won many to the faith.

In the persecution of Diocletian they were arrested, tortured, and beheaded, about the year 287, at Cyrrhus, which became the centre of their cult. Honoured as patrons of physicians and the sick, their names are inscribed in the Roman canon of the Mass.
saints.knownFor: Healing the sick without charge and their martyrdom for the faith.

saints.name: St. Vincent de Paul
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The Gascon priest who organized the charity of an age, gathering priests and laywomen to serve the poor, the galley-slave, and the foundling…
biography: Born to a peasant family in Gascony in 1581, Vincent was ordained young and, after a conversion to deeper zeal, gave his life to the poor. In 1625 he founded the Congregation of the Mission (the Vincentians) to preach in the countryside and form clergy, and organized parish charities across France.

With St. Louise de Marillac he founded the Daughters of Charity, sending sisters into the streets and hospitals, and he laboured for galley-slaves, abandoned children, and the victims of war. He died in 1660 and was canonized in 1737; his name remains a byword for organized Christian charity.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Vincentians and Daughters of Charity for the service of the poor.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 27 September

saints.name: St. Wenceslaus
saints.title: Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The Christian duke of Bohemia, raised by his holy grandmother, murdered at the church door by his own brother…
biography: Wenceslaus (Václav), duke of Bohemia, was formed in the faith by his grandmother St. Ludmila and, on coming to power, ruled as a just and devout Christian prince, favouring the Church and the poor and seeking peace with his neighbours. His piety and his policy toward the Germans made him enemies among the nobles.

He was set upon and killed by his own brother Boleslaus and his followers at the door of a church about the year 935. Venerated at once as a martyr, he became the patron and heavenly prince of the Czech people, his memory carried across Christendom in song.
saints.knownFor: His just Christian rule and his martyrdom at his brother's hand.

saints.name: Sts. Michael, Gabriel and Raphael
saints.title: Archangels
saints.shortBlurb: The three archangels named in Scripture — the warrior, the messenger, and the healer — honored together on Michaelmas…
biography: Three angels are named in the Scriptures. Michael, “who is like God,” leads the heavenly host against the dragon and is the guardian of the Church. Gabriel, “the strength of God,” announced the Incarnation to Mary and the birth of the Baptist to Zechariah. Raphael, “God heals,” accompanied Tobias on his journey and healed his father's blindness.
Their common feast, long kept as Michaelmas, honors the ministry of the angels in the plan of salvation.
saints.knownFor: The angelic ministry of protection, message, and healing.

saints.name: St. Jerome
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The fiery scholar of Bethlehem who gave the Latin Church its Bible, the Vulgate, translating the Scriptures from the original tongues…
biography: Born about 347 at Stridon in Dalmatia, Jerome was schooled in Rome and became the most learned scripture scholar of his age, mastering Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. At the request of Pope St. Damasus he undertook to revise and translate the Bible into Latin, the version that became the Vulgate.

He settled at Bethlehem, near the place of the Lord’s birth, where he wrote commentaries, defended the faith, and guided a community of monks and holy women until his death about 420. He is often shown with a lion, a skull, and his books.
saints.knownFor: The Vulgate; scripture scholarship; “Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ.”

canonization.canonized: Pre-Congregation; named a Doctor of the Church in 1298 by Pope Boniface VIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 September

saints.name: St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus
saints.title: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Little Flower of Carmel, who taught the “little way” of confidence and love and died at twenty-four…
biography: Marie-Françoise-Thérèse Martin entered the Carmel of Lisieux at fifteen and lived a hidden life of prayer and small acts of love, which she called her “little way” of spiritual childhood — trusting wholly in God's mercy rather than in great deeds. At her superior's bidding she wrote the memoir published as The Story of a Soul.
She died of tuberculosis at twenty-four, promising to “spend her heaven doing good upon earth.” Declared a Doctor of the Church, she is also a patron of the missions.
saints.knownFor: The “little way” of confidence and love.

canonization.canonized: 1925 by Pope Pius XI; Doctor of the Church (1997)

sources.text: Thérèse of Lisieux, The Story of a Soul (L'Histoire d'une âme, 1898; public domain)

saints.name: The Holy Guardian Angels
saints.title: Angelic Guardians
saints.shortBlurb: The heavenly guardians whom God appoints to watch over, protect, and pray for each human soul…
biography: The Church has always taught, on the witness of Scripture, that God assigns to each of the faithful an angel to guard body and soul. Our Lord himself speaks of the little ones whose angels “always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven,” and the Psalms declare that God has given his angels charge to keep us in all our ways.

A feast of the Guardian Angels was celebrated in various places from the sixteenth century and was extended to the universal Church by Pope Clement X in 1670. It is kept on the day after the feast of the Archangels, giving thanks for the unseen protection that accompanies every Christian through life.
saints.knownFor: God's appointment of an angel to guard each soul.

saints.name: Sts. Ewald the Fair and Ewald the Dark
saints.title: Priests and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two English priests, brothers distinguished only by the colour of their hair, martyred while preaching to the Old Saxons…
biography: The two Ewalds were English priests from Northumbria, both bearing the same name and told apart only as Ewald the Fair and Ewald the Dark. Trained in Ireland, they joined the missionary work among the continental Saxons that St. Willibrord had begun.

About the year 695 they crossed into the land of the Old Saxons to preach the Gospel. Fearing that the missionaries would turn their chief and people from the old gods, a group of pagans seized and killed them; the Venerable Bede records the honour later paid to their relics.
saints.knownFor: Martyrdom while evangelizing the Old Saxons.

saints.name: St. Francis of Assisi
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: The Poverello of Assisi, who wedded Lady Poverty, founded the Friars Minor, and bore in his own flesh the wounds of the Crucified…
biography: Born about 1181 to a wealthy cloth merchant of Assisi, Francis renounced his inheritance to follow Christ in poverty, hearing in a ruined chapel the command to “rebuild my church.” Companions gathered, and in 1209 Pope Innocent III approved his rule, the beginning of the Order of Friars Minor.

He preached penance and peace, loved all creatures as God’s handiwork, and composed the Canticle of the Sun. On Mount La Verna in 1224 he received the stigmata, the first recorded bearer of the wounds of Christ. He died at the Portiuncula on 3 October 1226.
saints.knownFor: Radical poverty; love of creation; the stigmata; the first Christmas crèche.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 October

saints.name: St. Faustina Kowalska
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A humble Polish sister and “secretary” of Divine Mercy, to whom Christ entrusted the message of his boundless mercy…
biography: Helena Kowalska was born near Łódź in Poland in 1905 and entered the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy, taking the name Maria Faustina. She worked as a cook, gardener, and portress, hiding a rich interior life beneath the most ordinary duties.

In a series of revelations she recorded in her Diary, she reported that Christ appeared to her asking that his mercy be proclaimed to the world, giving the image of the Divine Mercy and the chaplet. She died of tuberculosis in 1938; the devotion she promoted was later approved and the Sunday after Easter established as Divine Mercy Sunday.
saints.knownFor: The Divine Mercy devotion.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Maria Faustina Kowalska (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Bruno
saints.title: Priest and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A learned master of Reims who fled fame for the silence of the mountains and founded the Carthusian Order…
biography: Born at Cologne about 1030, Bruno became a celebrated teacher at Reims, numbering a future pope among his pupils. Repelled by ecclesiastical corruption and drawn to solitude, he withdrew with a few companions into the wild valley of the Chartreuse near Grenoble in 1084, founding there the first Carthusian hermitage.

Called to Rome to advise Pope Urban II, he declined a bishopric and instead established a second charterhouse in Calabria, where he died in 1101. The order he founded, uniting the hermit's solitude with a common life, is famed for never having required reform.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Carthusian Order.

canonization.canonized: Cultus approved 1514 by Pope Leo X; feast extended to the whole Church 1623

saints.name: Our Lady of the Rosary
saints.title: Memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: A memorial giving thanks for the Rosary and for the deliverance of Christendom at Lepanto…
biography: After the fleet of the Holy League defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto on 7 October 1571, Pope St. Pius V attributed the victory to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin invoked through the Rosary. He established a commemoration of Our Lady of Victory, which his successor Gregory XIII renamed the feast of the Holy Rosary.

Pope Clement XI extended the feast to the universal Church in 1716 after another victory over the Turks, and Leo XIII, the “Rosary Pope,” gave the devotion fresh prominence. The day recalls the Church's confidence in Mary's intercession and in the meditative prayer of the mysteries of Christ.
saints.knownFor: The Rosary and the deliverance at Lepanto.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Holy Rosary”

saints.name: St. Pelagia the Penitent
saints.title: Penitent
saints.shortBlurb: A celebrated dancer of Antioch who turned from a life of sin to a hidden life of penance…
biography: According to an ancient and widely told account, Pelagia was a famous and worldly actress and dancer of Antioch, renowned for her beauty and wealth. Moved by the preaching of a bishop named Nonnus, she was converted, received baptism, and gave away her possessions to the poor.

Seeking to bury her former life entirely, she is said to have withdrawn to a cell on the Mount of Olives near Jerusalem, living in penance and prayer in the disguise of a monk called Pelagius, her identity discovered only at her death. Her story was long cherished as a model of true conversion.
saints.knownFor: Conversion from a life of sin to penitential solitude.

saints.name: St. Denis and Companions
saints.title: Bishop and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The first bishop of Paris, martyred with his companions and honoured as an apostle of Gaul…
biography: Denis (Dionysius) was sent from Rome in the third century to evangelize Gaul and became the first bishop of Paris, preaching from an island in the Seine. With the priest Rusticus and the deacon Eleutherius he gathered a Christian community amid persecution.

During a persecution, most likely under the emperor Valerian about the year 258, the three were arrested, tortured, and beheaded on the hill north of the city long afterward called Montmartre, the “mount of the martyrs.” Denis became one of the great patrons of France, honoured at the royal abbey that bears his name.
saints.knownFor: First bishop of Paris and martyr of Gaul.

saints.name: St. Francis Borgia
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Spanish duke who, shaken by the sight of a dead empress's ruined beauty, left his rank to become a Jesuit…
biography: Born in 1510 into one of the most powerful families of Spain, Francis Borgia was Duke of Gandía and a courtier of the Emperor Charles V. Charged with escorting the body of the Empress Isabella to burial, he is said to have been so struck by the corruption of her once-celebrated beauty that he resolved to serve only a Sovereign who could never die.

After the death of his wife he entered the Society of Jesus, renouncing his titles, and rose to become the order's third Superior General. Under his guidance the young society expanded across Europe and into the missions of the New World; he died in Rome in 1572 and is often called a “second founder” of the Jesuits.
saints.knownFor: Renouncing a dukedom to serve as a Jesuit.

saints.name: St. John XXIII
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The “Good Pope” of peasant stock who, in a brief pontificate, summoned the Second Vatican Council…
biography: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was born in 1881 to a family of peasant farmers near Bergamo in northern Italy. As a papal diplomat during the Second World War he helped rescue many Jews, and later as Patriarch of Venice he won affection for his warmth and simplicity.

Elected pope in 1958 at the age of nearly seventy-seven and expected to be a caretaker, he startled the Church by convoking the Second Vatican Council to renew its life and open a dialogue with the modern world. Beloved as “Good Pope John,” he died in 1963 before the Council concluded.
saints.knownFor: Convoking the Second Vatican Council.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. John XXIII (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Wilfrid
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Northumbrian bishop who championed the customs of Rome and carried the faith to the pagan South Saxons…
biography: Born in Northumbria about 633, Wilfrid studied at Lindisfarne and Rome and became a forceful advocate of Roman usages against the older Celtic traditions of the North. At the Synod of Whitby in 664 his argument helped persuade King Oswiu to adopt the Roman method of calculating Easter, aligning the English Church with the wider West.

As bishop of York he founded monasteries and endured repeated exiles amid disputes with kings and fellow bishops, appealing more than once to Rome. In banishment he evangelized the still-pagan South Saxons of Sussex. He died in 709 and was honoured as one of the great churchmen of Anglo-Saxon England.
saints.knownFor: Championing Roman usages at the Synod of Whitby.

saints.name: St. Edward the Confessor
saints.title: King
saints.shortBlurb: The pious last king of the House of Wessex, remembered for gentleness, generosity, and the building of Westminster Abbey…
biography: Edward was born about 1003, a son of King Æthelred, and spent much of his youth in exile in Normandy before coming to the English throne in 1042. His reign was marked by a reputation for personal holiness, love of the poor, and a peaceable temper, so that he was surnamed “the Confessor.”

He rebuilt the great abbey church of Westminster, where he was buried after his death early in 1066, on the eve of the Norman Conquest. His shrine became a focus of English devotion, and his relics were solemnly translated on 13 October, the day now kept in his memory.
saints.knownFor: Piety as king and the founding of Westminster Abbey.

saints.name: St. Callistus I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A former slave who rose to govern the Roman Church and gave his name to its great catacomb…
biography: Callistus began life as a slave in Rome and, according to the tradition, was once condemned to hard labour in the mines of Sardinia before regaining his freedom. Trusted by Pope Zephyrinus, he was set over the Christian cemetery on the Appian Way that still bears his name, where many of the early popes were buried.

Elected pope about the year 217, he governed the Church through fierce controversies over penance and the readmission of grave sinners, showing a mercy that drew the anger of rigorists such as Hippolytus. He is honoured as a martyr, having died about 222 in a popular tumult.
saints.knownFor: Governing the Roman Church and its catacomb cemetery.

saints.name: St. Teresa of Jesus (Ávila)
saints.title: Virgin and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Carmelite of Ávila who reformed her order and mapped the soul's ascent to God in the Interior Castle…
biography: Teresa entered the Carmel at Ávila and, after years of struggle, received extraordinary graces of prayer. With St. John of the Cross she reformed the Carmelite order, founding the Discalced houses of stricter observance, and she wrote works of mystical theology — the Life, the Way of Perfection, and the Interior Castle — of enduring authority.
A woman of great practical sense as well as deep prayer, she died in 1582 and was the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.
saints.knownFor: Reforming Carmel and her writings on mystical prayer.

canonization.canonized: 1622 by Pope Gregory XV; Doctor of the Church (1970)

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 15 October

saints.name: St. Margaret Mary Alacoque
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: A Visitation nun of Paray-le-Monial to whom Christ revealed the riches of his Sacred Heart…
biography: Born in Burgundy in 1647, Margaret Mary entered the Visitation convent at Paray-le-Monial. There, between 1673 and 1675, she reported a series of revelations in which Christ showed her his Heart burning with love for humanity and asked for its devotion, for reparation, and for Communion on the First Fridays.

Her claims were met at first with distrust within her own community, but she found a defender in her confessor, the Jesuit St. Claude de la Colombière. Though she died in obscurity in 1690, the devotion to the Sacred Heart she promoted spread throughout the Church in the centuries after her death.
saints.knownFor: The revelations of the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

saints.name: St. Ignatius of Antioch
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A bishop of the apostolic age who wrote seven great letters on his way to the beasts at Rome…
biography: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch and a disciple of the Apostles, was condemned to the beasts and sent under guard to Rome. Along the way he wrote seven letters to the churches — precious witnesses to the early faith — urging unity around the bishop and the Eucharist, and begging the Romans not to hinder his martyrdom: “I am the wheat of God.”
He was thrown to the lions in the amphitheater about the year 107.
saints.knownFor: His letters on Church unity and the Eucharist; martyrdom at Rome.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 1 February

saints.name: St. Luke
saints.title: Evangelist
saints.shortBlurb: The “beloved physician,” companion of St. Paul, who wrote the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles…
biography: Luke, a Gentile physician called by Paul “the beloved physician,” was his companion on his journeys and stayed with him to the end. He wrote the third Gospel, which alone preserves the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son and the songs of the infancy, and its sequel, the Acts of the Apostles.
Tradition honors him as a painter of the Virgin; his symbol is the winged ox, patron of physicians and artists.
saints.knownFor: Writing the third Gospel and the Acts of the Apostles.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 18 October

saints.name: Sts. John de Brébeuf and Isaac Jogues, and Companions
saints.title: Priests and Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The North American Martyrs, French Jesuits who carried the Gospel to the Huron and Iroquois and died for it…
biography: The eight North American Martyrs were French Jesuit missionaries and lay helpers who labored among the Huron and neighboring peoples of New France in the seventeenth century. Isaac Jogues, tortured and mutilated, returned to his mission and was slain in 1646; John de Brébeuf, the great apostle to the Huron, endured a long and cruel martyrdom in 1649.
They and their companions gave their lives between 1642 and 1649. They are patrons of the Americas and of Canada.
saints.knownFor: Martyrdom while evangelizing the peoples of North America.

sources.text: R. G. Thwaites (ed.), The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents (1896–1901; public domain)

saints.name: St. Paul of the Cross
saints.title: Priest and Founder
saints.shortBlurb: A mystic of the Passion who founded the Passionists to keep the sufferings of Christ before the world…
biography: Paul Francis Danei was born at Ovada in northern Italy in 1694. After a period of intense prayer and inspiration he composed a rule for a new congregation devoted to preaching and meditating on the Passion of Christ, and in time founded the Congregation of the Passion, whose members add a fourth vow to keep alive the memory of the sufferings of the Lord.

He spent nearly fifty years as a missionary preacher through the towns and countryside of Italy, renowned for the power of his sermons and for his gifts in prayer. He died in Rome in 1775 and was canonized by Pope Pius IX in 1867.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Passionists and preaching the Passion.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Paul of the Cross”

saints.name: St. Hilarion
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: The father of monastic life in Palestine, a disciple of St. Anthony whose life St. Jerome recorded…
biography: Born of pagan parents near Gaza about 291, Hilarion was converted while studying at Alexandria and sought out the great hermit St. Anthony in the Egyptian desert. Returning home, he gave away his inheritance and took up a life of extreme austerity in the wilderness near the sea, becoming the first to plant the anchoritic life in Palestine.

Disciples gathered around him and monasteries multiplied, but fleeing the crowds that his reputed miracles attracted, he wandered through Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia, and at last Cyprus, where he died about 371. His life was written soon afterward by St. Jerome, who prized him as a model of the solitary vocation.
saints.knownFor: Bringing the monastic life to Palestine.

saints.name: St. John Paul II
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The Polish pope of “Be not afraid,” whose long and missionary pontificate reshaped the modern Church…
biography: Karol Wojtyła was born at Wadowice in Poland in 1920 and came of age under the Nazi occupation, working in a quarry and studying for the priesthood in secret. As Archbishop of Kraków he took a leading part in the Second Vatican Council, and in 1978 he was elected the first non-Italian pope in more than four centuries.

For nearly twenty-seven years he governed the Church, traveling to well over a hundred countries, calling the young to holiness, defending human dignity, and contributing to the peaceful fall of communism in his homeland. He suffered the last years of his life in public frailty and died in 2005; the day kept in his honour marks the inauguration of his pontificate.
saints.knownFor: His long, missionary pontificate and defense of human dignity.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. John Paul II (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. John of Capistrano
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Franciscan preacher and reformer who, at seventy, rallied the defenders of Belgrade against the Turks…
biography: Born at Capestrano in the Abruzzi in 1386, John trained as a lawyer and served as governor of Perugia before a term of imprisonment turned him to God; he entered the Friars Minor and became one of the most powerful preachers of his age. With St. Bernardine of Siena he worked for the reform of the Franciscan Observants and traveled across Europe drawing great crowds.

In his old age he was sent to preach against the advancing Ottoman armies, and in 1456 he helped inspire and lead the Christian forces who broke the siege of Belgrade. Worn out by his labors, he died a few months later. He was canonized in 1690 and is honoured as a patron of military chaplains.
saints.knownFor: Preaching reform and rallying the defense of Belgrade.

saints.name: St. Anthony Mary Claret
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Catalan weaver's son turned tireless missionary, founder of the Claretians and archbishop of Santiago de Cuba…
biography: Born in 1807 at Sallent in Catalonia, the son of a weaver, Anthony Mary Claret was ordained a priest and gave himself to popular missions and to the spread of good books, founding a religious congregation now known as the Claretians. In 1850 he was made Archbishop of Santiago de Cuba, where he reformed the Church and endured attempts on his life.

Recalled to Spain as confessor to Queen Isabella II, he was drawn into the turmoil of court and revolution and followed the queen into exile. A man of ceaseless preaching, writing, and prayer, he died in exile in France in 1870 and was canonized in 1950.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Claretians and his tireless preaching.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Anthony Mary Claret (vatican.va)

saints.name: Sts. Crispin and Crispinian
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Two brothers who preached the Gospel by day and made shoes by night, martyred at Soissons…
biography: According to their ancient legend, Crispin and Crispinian were brothers, perhaps of noble Roman birth, who came to Gaul to spread the Christian faith. Settling at Soissons, they supported themselves and gave to the poor by working as shoemakers, preaching to those who came to them.

During the persecution under the emperor Diocletian they were arrested, tortured, and put to death about the year 286. They became the beloved patrons of shoemakers, cobblers, and leatherworkers, and their feast, “Saint Crispin's Day,” long held a place in popular memory.
saints.knownFor: Working as shoemakers while preaching the Gospel.

saints.name: St. Cedd
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A Northumbrian monk trained at Lindisfarne who evangelized the East Saxons and founded Lastingham…
biography: Cedd was one of four brothers, among them St. Chad, raised and trained in the monastic life at Lindisfarne under St. Aidan. Sent first to the Middle Angles and then to the kingdom of the East Saxons, he preached with such success that he was consecrated their bishop, founding churches and monasteries along the way.

He took part in the Synod of Whitby in 664 and, though schooled in the Celtic tradition, accepted its decision for the Roman observance. Later that year, at the monastery he had established at Lastingham in Yorkshire, he died of the plague. The Venerable Bede preserved his memory.
saints.knownFor: Evangelizing the East Saxons and founding Lastingham.

sources.text: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (public domain)

saints.name: St. Frumentius
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A shipwrecked youth who became the apostle and first bishop of Ethiopia…
biography: According to the ancient historians, Frumentius and his brother Aedesius, boys from Tyre, were the survivors of a shipwreck on the Red Sea coast and were carried to the court of the king of Axum in Ethiopia. Rising to positions of trust, Frumentius encouraged the Christian merchants there and prepared the way for the conversion of the land.

Traveling to Alexandria, he asked St. Athanasius to send a bishop for the growing Church, and Athanasius consecrated Frumentius himself for the task. Returning to Ethiopia, he baptized the king and countless others, so that he is honoured as the apostle of that nation and its first bishop, remembered by the Ethiopians as “Abba Salama,” Father of Peace.
saints.knownFor: Bringing Christianity to Ethiopia.

saints.name: Sts. Simon and Jude
saints.title: Apostles
saints.shortBlurb: Two of the Twelve honored together — Simon the Zealot and Jude Thaddaeus, invoked in desperate causes…
biography: Simon, called the Zealot, and Jude, called Thaddaeus, are named among the Twelve Apostles. Jude is the author of the short Epistle that bears his name and, by long popular devotion, the patron of hopeless and desperate causes. Of their preaching little is recorded with certainty; ancient tradition joins them in mission to Persia, where they were martyred together.
They share this feast in the Roman calendar.
saints.knownFor: Apostolic preaching; Jude, patron of desperate causes.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 28 October

saints.name: St. Narcissus of Jerusalem
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A bishop of Jerusalem famed for holiness and miracles who lived to an extreme old age…
biography: Narcissus became bishop of Jerusalem in the latter part of the second century, already advanced in years. Eusebius, the early historian, records the veneration in which he was held and the wonders attributed to him, among them the changing of water into oil for the lamps of the church one Easter vigil.

Slandered by his enemies, he withdrew for a time into solitude, but was restored to his people when the falsehood was exposed. He is said to have governed his church to well past the age of a hundred, and to have shared its rule at the last with St. Alexander. He was honoured after his death as a model of endurance and holiness.
saints.knownFor: His long episcopate and holiness at Jerusalem.

saints.name: St. Alphonsus Rodríguez
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A widowed merchant who became a Jesuit doorkeeper and found sanctity in a humble office faithfully kept…
biography: Born at Segovia in Spain in 1532, Alphonsus inherited his father's cloth business, married, and raised a family, only to be left a widower after the successive deaths of his wife and children. Turning wholly to God, he sought entrance to the Society of Jesus and, lacking learning, was received as a lay brother.

For nearly half a century he served as porter, or doorkeeper, at the Jesuit college of Montesión on the island of Majorca, greeting every visitor as though greeting Christ himself. His hidden holiness and spiritual counsel drew many, among them the young St. Peter Claver, whom he urged to the missions of the New World. He died in 1617 and was canonized in 1888.
saints.knownFor: Sanctity in the humble office of doorkeeper.

saints.name: St. Wolfgang
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: A monk and reforming bishop of Regensburg who tutored a future emperor and served the poor…
biography: Born in Swabia about 934 and educated at the abbey of Reichenau, Wolfgang taught in the cathedral school of Trier before becoming a Benedictine monk. In 972 he was made bishop of Regensburg in Bavaria, where he reformed the monasteries, restored discipline among the clergy, and cared generously for the poor.

He served for a time as tutor to the young Henry, later the emperor St. Henry II. Renowned for learning, austerity, and preaching, he died in 994 while traveling and was buried at Regensburg. He was canonized in 1052 and became one of the most popular saints of medieval Germany.
saints.knownFor: Reforming his diocese and tutoring an emperor.

saints.name: All Saints
saints.title: Solemnity of All the Saints
saints.shortBlurb: The Church's great feast of all the blessed in heaven, known and unknown, who share the vision of God…
biography: On this solemnity the Church honours the whole company of the saints in glory — not only those named in her calendar, but the countless multitude of the redeemed whom no one can number, drawn from every nation and age. The feast celebrates the communion of saints, the bond of prayer and charity uniting the pilgrim Church on earth with the Church triumphant in heaven.

A commemoration of all the martyrs was kept in Rome from early centuries; Pope Boniface IV dedicated the Pantheon to Our Lady and all the martyrs in the seventh century, and Pope Gregory IV is traditionally said to have fixed the general feast on 1 November in the ninth century, whence it spread throughout the Western Church.
saints.knownFor: Honouring the whole multitude of the blessed in heaven.

saints.name: The Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed
saints.title: All Souls' Day
saints.shortBlurb: The day the Church prays for all the faithful departed still being purified before they enter the joy of heaven…
biography: On All Souls' Day the Church remembers in prayer, sacrifice, and almsgiving all the faithful departed — the souls in purgatory who have died in God's grace but are not yet fully purified. It expresses the ancient Christian conviction that the living may aid the dead by their intercession, above all through the offering of the Mass.

The general commemoration was established for the monasteries of Cluny by their abbot St. Odilo near the end of the tenth century, fixed on the day after All Saints, and was gradually adopted by the whole Western Church. Priests are permitted to offer three Masses on this day for the departed.
saints.knownFor: Prayer and sacrifice offered for the souls in purgatory.

saints.name: St. Martin de Porres
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: A Dominican lay brother of Lima whose charity to the poor and the sick knew no barrier of race or rank…
biography: Born at Lima in Peru in 1579, the son of a Spanish gentleman and a freed woman of African descent, Martin was apprenticed to a barber-surgeon before entering the Dominican priory of Lima as a lay helper, later becoming a professed lay brother. Humble, penitential, and tireless, he served as infirmarian and almoner, caring for the sick of every class and founding relief for the poor and for orphans.

He was famed in his own lifetime for his charity, his love of the sick and of animals, and for extraordinary graces. He died at Lima on 3 November 1639. He is a patron of those working for interracial harmony and of the poor.
saints.knownFor: Heroic charity to the poor and the sick as a Dominican lay brother.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Martin de Porres (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Charles Borromeo
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The reforming Archbishop of Milan who turned the decrees of the Council of Trent into pastoral fact…
biography: Born in 1538 of a noble Lombard family and nephew of Pope Pius IV, Charles was made a cardinal and administrator of Milan while still young. As the pope's close counsellor he laboured for the successful conclusion of the Council of Trent, and thereafter he devoted himself to carrying its reforms into practice.

As Archbishop of Milan he founded seminaries for the training of priests, held synods, catechized the young, visited the remotest parishes of his vast diocese, and gave himself heroically to the plague-stricken of Milan in 1576. Worn out by labour and penance, he died on 4 November 1584. He is a patron of bishops, seminarians, and catechists.
saints.knownFor: Reforming the Church after Trent as Archbishop of Milan.

saints.name: Sts. Zachary and Elizabeth
saints.title: Parents of St. John the Baptist
saints.shortBlurb: The righteous priest and his wife, kinswoman of the Virgin Mary, who in old age became parents of the Baptist…
biography: Zachary was a priest of the course of Abia, and his wife Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron and a kinswoman of the Blessed Virgin Mary. The Gospel of Luke calls them both just before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments, yet childless and advanced in years.

To Zachary, ministering in the Temple, the angel Gabriel announced the birth of a son, John, forerunner of the Lord; struck dumb for his hesitation, he regained speech at the child's naming and sang the Benedictus. It was to Elizabeth, then with child, that Mary came in haste, and Elizabeth greeted her as the mother of her Lord. The Roman Martyrology commemorates them on this day.
saints.knownFor: The devout parents of St. John the Baptist.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Leonard of Noblac
saints.title: Hermit
saints.shortBlurb: A Frankish hermit near Limoges long invoked by prisoners and by women in childbirth…
biography: According to his medieval life, Leonard was a Frankish nobleman of the court of King Clovis who was converted and instructed by St. Remigius of Reims. Refusing worldly honours, he withdrew to the forest of Noblac near Limoges, where he lived as a hermit and gathered disciples, founding the monastery that bears his name.

He was renowned for obtaining the release of captives and prisoners, who by tradition brought their chains to his shrine, and for his intercession on behalf of women in labour. His cult spread widely across France, Germany, and beyond in the Middle Ages. He is a patron of prisoners and of expectant mothers.
saints.knownFor: Intercession for prisoners and women in childbirth.

saints.name: St. Willibrord
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The Northumbrian monk who became the Apostle of the Frisians and first Archbishop of Utrecht…
biography: Born in Northumbria about 658 and formed in the monastery of Ripon and among the Irish in Ireland, Willibrord crossed to the Continent in 690 with a band of companions to preach the Gospel to the pagan Frisians. Consecrated bishop of the Frisians by Pope Sergius I in Rome in 695, he fixed his see at Utrecht.

For more than forty years he evangelized the Low Countries, founding churches and the great monastery of Echternach, which became the centre of his mission and his burial place. He died on 7 November 739. He is honoured as the Apostle of the Frisians and a patron of the Netherlands and Luxembourg.
saints.knownFor: The evangelization of Frisia and the see of Utrecht.

saints.name: The Four Crowned Martyrs
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: Roman martyrs of the Diocletian persecution honoured on the Caelian Hill from the earliest centuries…
biography: The Quattuor Coronati are among the most anciently venerated martyrs of Rome, commemorated on the Caelian Hill where the basilica of the Santi Quattro Coronati still stands. Their traditions are intertwined: one names four soldiers or officials put to death under Diocletian for refusing to worship the pagan god Aesculapius.

A second account, joined to their feast, honours a group of Pannonian stonemasons — Claudius, Nicostratus, Symphorian, Castorius, and Simplicius — who suffered death rather than carve an idol for the emperor. Whatever the exact history behind the names, their cult in Rome is very old, and they were long invoked as patrons of sculptors and stonemasons.
saints.knownFor: Ancient Roman martyrs venerated as patrons of stonemasons.

saints.name: The Dedication of the Lateran Basilica
saints.title: The Mother Church of Rome and of the World
saints.shortBlurb: The feast of the Lateran, cathedral of the Bishop of Rome and mother of all the churches of the city and the world…
biography: This feast honours the dedication of the Basilica of the Most Holy Saviour and of Sts. John the Baptist and John the Evangelist at the Lateran, the cathedral church of the Pope as Bishop of Rome. An inscription on its façade names it the mother and head of all the churches of the city and of the world.

The basilica arose in the fourth century on land given by the Emperor Constantine and was long the residence of the popes. Its feast, kept throughout the Western Church, is a celebration of the unity of the whole Church around the See of Peter rather than of any one saint.
saints.knownFor: The cathedral of the Pope, mother of all churches.

saints.name: St. Leo the Great
saints.title: Pope and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The pope whose Tome guided the Council of Chalcedon and who turned back Attila from the gates of Rome…
biography: Leo became Bishop of Rome in 440 and governed the Church through a time of doctrinal strife and barbarian invasion. His dogmatic letter, the Tome of Leo, set forth the true faith of the two natures in the one person of Christ and was acclaimed by the Council of Chalcedon in 451 as the voice of Peter.

In 452 he went out to meet Attila the Hun and persuaded him to spare Rome, and later interceded with the Vandals who sacked the city. A vigorous defender of the primacy of the Roman See and a great preacher, he died on 10 November 461 and was later declared a Doctor of the Church.
saints.knownFor: The Tome of Leo and the defence of the faith at Chalcedon.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church (1754)

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Leo I (the Great)”

saints.name: St. Martin of Tours
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The soldier who cut his cloak for a beggar, then left the army to become a monk and bishop of Tours…
biography: Martin, a soldier of the Roman army, met a shivering beggar at the gate of Amiens and cut his own cloak in two to clothe him; that night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given. Baptized, he left military service, founded one of the first monasteries in Gaul, and was made bishop of Tours against his wish.
He labored to convert the countryside and became one of the most beloved saints of the West; his shrine at Tours was a great center of pilgrimage.
saints.knownFor: Sharing his cloak with a beggar; monk and bishop of Gaul.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 November

saints.name: St. Josaphat
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The Ruthenian archbishop and monk who gave his life for the union of the Eastern Church with Rome…
biography: Born about 1580 at Volodymyr in Volhynia and baptized John Kuncevyc, he became a monk of the Byzantine rite and took the name Josaphat, embracing the Union of Brest by which many Ruthenians were reconciled with the See of Rome while keeping their Eastern liturgy. He was made Archbishop of Polotsk.

His zeal for the union drew fierce opposition, and on 12 November 1623 he was killed by a mob at Vitebsk, dying a martyr for Christian unity. He was the first saint of the Eastern Church to be formally canonized by Rome. He is honoured as a patron of Christian unity between East and West.
saints.knownFor: Martyrdom for the union of the Eastern churches with Rome.

saints.name: St. Frances Xavier Cabrini
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The Italian foundress who crossed the ocean to serve immigrants and became the first United States citizen canonized…
biography: Born in 1850 near Lodi in Lombardy, Frances Cabrini founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in 1880. Longing to be a missionary, she was directed by Pope Leo XIII not to the East but to the West, to care for the poor Italian immigrants pouring into the Americas.

Arriving in New York in 1889, she and her sisters founded schools, hospitals, and orphanages across the United States and in Central and South America, some sixty-seven institutions in all. A naturalized American citizen, she died in Chicago in 1917. Canonized in 1946, she is the patroness of immigrants.
saints.knownFor: Founding schools and hospitals for immigrants in the Americas.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Frances Xavier Cabrini (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Lawrence O'Toole
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: The reforming Archbishop of Dublin who shepherded his people through the Norman conquest of Ireland…
biography: Born about 1128, Lorcán Ua Tuathail was abbot of Glendalough before he was chosen Archbishop of Dublin in 1162. A reformer and a friend of the poor, he laboured to renew the discipline of clergy and people and was noted for his personal austerity and charity.

He guided Dublin through the turmoil of the Anglo-Norman invasion, acting as mediator between the Irish and the newcomers, and took part in the Third Lateran Council in 1179. He died at Eu in Normandy on 14 November 1180 while on an embassy of peace. He is the patron saint of the Archdiocese of Dublin.
saints.knownFor: Reform of the Church and peacemaking during the Norman invasion.

saints.name: St. Albert the Great
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The Dominican polymath and teacher of Thomas Aquinas, called the Universal Doctor…
biography: Born about 1200 at Lauingen in Swabia, Albert entered the Order of Preachers and became one of the most learned men of the Middle Ages, mastering theology, philosophy, and the natural sciences with such range that he was called Doctor Universalis. At Paris and Cologne he taught the young Thomas Aquinas, whose genius he was the first to recognize and defend.

He served for a time as Bishop of Regensburg before returning to his studies and teaching, and he laboured to reconcile the newly recovered philosophy of Aristotle with Christian faith. He died at Cologne on 15 November 1280. He is a patron of natural scientists and students.
saints.knownFor: Uniting the natural sciences with theology and teaching St. Thomas Aquinas.

canonization.canonized: 1931 by Pope Pius XI, who declared him a Doctor of the Church

saints.name: St. Margaret of Scotland
saints.title: Queen
saints.shortBlurb: The saintly queen who reformed the Church of Scotland and gave herself to prayer and the poor…
biography: Born about 1045 of the exiled English royal house and raised in Hungary, Margaret came to Scotland and married King Malcolm III around 1070. A wife and mother of eight children — among them a king who became St. David and a queen of England — she united a devout private life of prayer, fasting, and reading with tireless charity to orphans and the poor.

She worked to reform the customs and worship of the Scottish Church, promoted synods, founded and restored churches, and softened the manners of the court. She died at Edinburgh on 16 November 1093, only days after her husband and eldest son fell in battle. She is a patroness of Scotland.
saints.knownFor: Reform of the Scottish Church and her charity as queen.

saints.name: St. Elizabeth of Hungary
saints.title: Religious
saints.shortBlurb: The young princess and widow who spent herself and her wealth on the sick and the poor…
biography: Daughter of King Andrew II of Hungary, Elizabeth was born in 1207 and married Louis IV, Landgrave of Thuringia. A devoted wife and mother, she was known for her ardent charity, building a hospital below the Wartburg and serving the sick and poor with her own hands; the legend of the loaves that turned to roses grew from this love.

Widowed in 1227 when Louis died on crusade, she embraced the poverty of the Third Order of St. Francis, renounced the comforts of the court, and gave herself wholly to the care of the destitute at Marburg. Worn out by penance and service, she died there on 17 November 1231, aged only twenty-four. She is a patroness of the Third Order Franciscans and of charitable works.
saints.knownFor: Her charity to the poor and sick as a widowed Franciscan tertiary.

saints.name: St. Rose Philippine Duchesne
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The French missionary of the Sacred Heart who carried Catholic education to the American frontier…
biography: Born at Grenoble in 1769, Rose Philippine Duchesne joined the Society of the Sacred Heart under its foundress St. Madeleine Sophie Barat, longing all the while to be a missionary. In 1818 she sailed to America and, on the Missouri frontier, opened at St. Charles the first free school west of the Mississippi.

For decades she founded schools, convents, and orphanages amid great hardship. Late in life she went to live among the Potawatomi, who, seeing her constant prayer, called her the woman who prays always. She died at St. Charles in 1852. Canonized in 1988, she is honoured in the United States on this day.
saints.knownFor: Pioneering Catholic education on the American frontier.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Rose Philippine Duchesne (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Mechtilde of Hackeborn
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The Benedictine nun of Helfta whose visions of the Heart of Christ were treasured by St. Gertrude the Great…
biography: Born about 1241 of a noble Saxon family, Mechtilde entered the monastery of Helfta, where her elder sister Gertrude of Hackeborn was abbess. Gifted with a beautiful voice, she led the choir and was called by her sisters the nightingale of Christ, and she became a wise and beloved mistress and guide of souls.

She was the spiritual teacher of the younger St. Gertrude the Great, and it was Gertrude and another sister who set down Mechtilde's mystical graces in the Book of Special Grace, a work rich in devotion to the Sacred Heart. She died at Helfta in 1298.
saints.knownFor: The mystical revelations recorded in the Book of Special Grace.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Edmund the Martyr
saints.title: King and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The king of East Anglia who chose death rather than deny Christ or betray his Christian people…
biography: Edmund was king of the East Angles in the ninth century, remembered as a just and devout ruler. When the invading Danish army overran his kingdom, he was defeated, taken captive, and pressed to renounce his faith and rule as a vassal under a heathen overlord.

Refusing to abandon Christ or to abandon his people to unbelievers, he was, according to tradition, bound to a tree, shot through with arrows, and beheaded on 20 November 869. His body was later enshrined at the great abbey of Bury St Edmunds, and he was long venerated as a patron of England.
saints.knownFor: Dying rather than deny Christ under the Danish invaders.

saints.name: The Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Memorial of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The memorial of Mary's dedication to God in the Temple as a young girl, all her life consecrated to the Lord…
biography: This memorial commemorates the presentation of the child Mary in the Temple of Jerusalem, where, by ancient tradition, she was offered to God and consecrated to his service. The account is drawn not from the canonical Gospels but from early Christian tradition, especially the Protoevangelium of James.

The feast arose in the Christian East and was gradually received into the Western calendar. Its meaning is less a single historical scene than the whole truth it expresses: that Mary was wholly given to God from her earliest years, the living temple prepared for the coming of the Lord.
saints.knownFor: Mary's consecration to God from her childhood.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Feast of the Presentation of Mary”

saints.name: St. Cecilia
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A Roman virgin and martyr of the early Church, honored from ancient times as the patroness of music…
biography: Cecilia, according to her ancient acts, was a noble Roman maiden who had consecrated her virginity to God and who won her husband Valerian and his brother to the faith; all were martyred in the persecutions. She is said to have sung to God in her heart even amid her wedding, and from this she became the patroness of sacred music.
Her name is in the Roman Canon of the Mass, and the great basilica in Trastevere marks the site venerated as her house.
saints.knownFor: Her martyrdom; patroness of music.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 22 November

saints.name: St. Clement I
saints.title: Pope and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: One of the first successors of St. Peter, whose letter to Corinth is among the oldest Christian writings after the New Testament…
biography: Clement was one of the earliest bishops of Rome, counted third in succession after St. Peter, and reigned near the close of the first century. His letter to the Church of Corinth, written to heal a division there, is one of the most precious documents of the sub-apostolic age and an early witness to the authority of the Roman Church.

According to tradition he was exiled and put to death under the Emperor Trajan, cast into the sea bound to an anchor, which became his emblem. His name too is remembered in the Roman Canon, and his supposed relics were later brought to Rome and enshrined in the basilica of San Clemente.
saints.knownFor: His early letter to the Corinthians and his witness as an apostolic pope.

saints.name: St. Andrew Dung-Lac and Companions
saints.title: Martyrs
saints.shortBlurb: The many martyrs of Vietnam — priests, catechists, and laity — who died for the faith across three centuries of persecution…
biography: This memorial honours a great company of martyrs who died for the Christian faith in Vietnam between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, during fierce persecutions under a succession of emperors. Among them were Vietnamese diocesan priests, catechists, and lay men and women, together with European missionaries of the Dominicans and the Paris Foreign Missions.

Their representative, Andrew Dũng-Lạc, was a Vietnamese priest beheaded in 1839. One hundred and seventeen of these martyrs were canonized together in 1988, and through them the whole multitude of Vietnam's witnesses is remembered. They are honoured as patrons of the Church in Vietnam.
saints.knownFor: The witness of the Vietnamese martyrs under persecution.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Martyrs of Vietnam (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Catherine of Alexandria
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A learned virgin-martyr of the early Church, honoured as a patroness of philosophers and students…
biography: According to her ancient and much-loved passion, Catherine was a young and highly educated Christian noblewoman of Alexandria in the early fourth century. Brought before the emperor during a persecution, she is said to have confuted the pagan philosophers summoned to refute her, converting some of them to Christ.

Condemned to die upon a spiked wheel that, tradition says, broke at her touch, she was at last beheaded; her body was later venerated at the great monastery on Mount Sinai. One of the Fourteen Holy Helpers, she is invoked as a patroness of philosophers, students, and those who work with wheels.
saints.knownFor: Confounding pagan philosophers and dying for the faith.

saints.name: St. Leonard of Port Maurice
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: The great Franciscan missionary preacher of Italy who spread the devotion of the Stations of the Cross…
biography: Born at Porto Maurizio on the Ligurian coast in 1676, Leonard became a Franciscan of the Strict Observance and the most celebrated popular preacher of eighteenth-century Italy. Travelling from town to town, he gave parish missions and retreats that drew immense crowds and renewed the fervour of the people.

He did more than anyone to spread the devotion of the Way of the Cross, erecting hundreds of sets of Stations throughout Italy, including, by tradition, within the Colosseum in Rome. He also ardently promoted the doctrine of the Immaculate Conception. He died in Rome in 1751 and is a patron of parish missions and preachers.
saints.knownFor: Popular missions and the spread of the Stations of the Cross.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Leonard of Port Maurice”

saints.name: St. Virgil of Salzburg
saints.title: Bishop
saints.shortBlurb: An Irish monk and man of learning who became Bishop of Salzburg and Apostle of Carinthia…
biography: Virgil, whose Irish name was Fergal, was a monk and scholar who left Ireland for the Continent in the eighth century. After a time at the court of Pepin, he came to Bavaria and was placed over the church of Salzburg, of which he became bishop, building its first cathedral and sending missionaries to the pagan Slavs of Carinthia.

A man of wide learning, he was noted for his knowledge of cosmology and famously held that the earth was a sphere with inhabited antipodes, a view that drew the suspicion of St. Boniface but did not condemn him. He died at Salzburg on 27 November 784 and is honoured as the Apostle of Carinthia.
saints.knownFor: The see of Salzburg and the evangelization of Carinthia.

saints.name: St. Catherine Labouré
saints.title: Virgin
saints.shortBlurb: The humble Daughter of Charity to whom Our Lady entrusted the Miraculous Medal…
biography: Born in Burgundy in 1806, Catherine Labouré entered the Daughters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul in Paris. In 1830, in the convent chapel of the Rue du Bac, she received a series of apparitions of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who asked that a medal be struck according to the image she showed — the medal that became known as the Miraculous Medal.

Keeping her role as visionary hidden, she spent the next forty-six years in obscurity, humbly caring for the aged and the sick at a hospice on the edge of Paris. Only after her death in 1876 was her identity widely known. Canonized in 1947, she is remembered for her hiddenness and her devotion to Our Lady.
saints.knownFor: The apparitions that gave the Church the Miraculous Medal.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Catherine Labouré (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Saturninus of Toulouse
saints.title: Bishop and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: The first bishop of Toulouse, dragged to his death by a bull for refusing to worship idols…
biography: Saturninus, called Sernin in his own city, was the first bishop of Toulouse in Gaul, sent to preach the Gospel in the third century. He is remembered for his fearless proclamation of Christ and for drawing many from the worship of the pagan gods.

According to his ancient passion, when he refused to offer sacrifice he was bound to a bull being led to the altar and dragged to his death down the steps of the Capitol, about the year 257. The church of Notre-Dame du Taur marks the place of his martyrdom, and his relics rest in the great basilica of Saint-Sernin at Toulouse.
saints.knownFor: The first bishop and martyr of Toulouse.

saints.name: St. Andrew
saints.title: Apostle
saints.shortBlurb: The brother of Simon Peter, first-called of the Apostles, who brought others to Christ and died on the X-shaped cross…
biography: Andrew, a fisherman of Bethsaida and brother of Simon Peter, was first a disciple of John the Baptist and, hearing him point to the Lamb of God, followed Jesus and brought his brother to Him — whence he is called the First-Called. He appears in the Gospels bringing others to Christ, the boy with the loaves and the inquiring Greeks.
Tradition holds that he preached in Greece and was crucified at Patras on a cross in the form of an X. He is the patron of Scotland, Greece, and Russia.
saints.knownFor: The first-called Apostle who brought others to Christ.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 30 November

saints.name: St. Edmund Campion
saints.title: Priest and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: An Oxford scholar who became a Jesuit and returned in secret to Elizabethan England, where he was betrayed, racked, and hanged for the faith…
biography: Edmund Campion was born in London in 1540 and rose as one of the most brilliant scholars of Oxford, so promising that Queen Elizabeth herself took notice of him. Drawn to the Catholic faith, he left England, was reconciled to the Church, and in Rome entered the newly founded Society of Jesus, being ordained a priest at Prague.

In 1580 he returned to England on the perilous Jesuit mission, ministering in secret to persecuted Catholics and circulating his bold written challenge to debate. Betrayed and arrested in 1581, he was imprisoned in the Tower of London, repeatedly racked, condemned on a charge of treason, and hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn on 1 December 1581.
saints.knownFor: The most celebrated of the English Jesuit martyrs under Elizabeth I.

canonization.canonized: 1970 by Pope Paul VI, among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Chromatius of Aquileia
saints.title: Bishop of Aquileia
saints.shortBlurb: The bishop of Aquileia and biblical commentator who befriended Jerome and worked as a craftsman of peace in a troubled age…
biography: Chromatius became bishop of Aquileia in northern Italy about the year 388 and made his city a center of learning and orthodoxy. A friend and patron of St. Jerome, he encouraged and helped support Jerome's biblical labors, and he sought to reconcile Jerome with their mutual friend Rufinus when the two were divided over the writings of Origen.

He left commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew and homilies still valued today, and he consoled and defended his people amid the disorders that came with the invasion of Italy by Alaric. He died about the year 407.
saints.knownFor: Bishop of Aquileia, biblical commentator, and friend of St. Jerome.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Francis Xavier
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A companion of Ignatius Loyola and the greatest missionary since the Apostles, who carried the Gospel to India and Japan…
biography: Born in the castle of Xavier in Navarre in 1506, Francis was won for God at the University of Paris by St. Ignatius of Loyola and became one of the first Jesuits. Sent to the East as papal legate, he labored from 1542 among the peoples of India, the Malay archipelago, and Japan, baptizing many thousands and founding enduring Christian communities.

Worn out by his travels, he died in 1552 on the island of Shangchuan within sight of the coast of China, which he had longed to enter. He is honored as the patron of the missions and of all who carry the Gospel to distant lands.
saints.knownFor: The Apostle of the Indies and of Japan.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 3 December

saints.name: St. John Damascene
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A monk of the Judean desert whose defense of holy images and vast synthesis of the faith earned him the title Doctor of the Church…
biography: John was born about 675 into a Christian family of Damascus and served, as his father had, in the administration of the Muslim caliph before leaving all to become a monk at the laura of Mar Saba near Jerusalem. From there, beyond the reach of the emperor, he wrote his great defense of the veneration of sacred images against the iconoclasts.

His masterwork, The Fount of Knowledge, gathered and ordered the teaching of the Greek Fathers and became a foundation of later theology in both East and West. He died about 749 and was declared a Doctor of the Church in 1890.
saints.knownFor: Defending sacred images and summing up the theology of the Greek Fathers.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; declared Doctor of the Church in 1890 by Pope Leo XIII

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 4 December

saints.name: St. Sabbas
saints.title: Abbot
saints.shortBlurb: A father of Eastern monasticism who founded the Great Lavra above the Kidron valley and defended the faith of Chalcedon…
biography: Sabbas was born in Cappadocia in 439 and as a young man went to Palestine, where he embraced the monastic life under St. Euthymius. In 483 he founded in the desert gorge near Jerusalem the Great Lavra, later called Mar Saba, which became the most famous monastery of the Holy Land and endures to this day.

Widely revered for holiness and wisdom, he was sent twice to Constantinople to plead the cause of orthodoxy and of his people, and he upheld the Council of Chalcedon against its opponents. He died at the Lavra in 532.
saints.knownFor: Founder of the Great Lavra (Mar Saba) and father of Palestinian monasticism.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 5 December

saints.name: St. Nicholas
saints.title: Bishop of Myra
saints.shortBlurb: The fourth-century bishop of Myra whose renown for secret generosity made him, in legend and love, the patron of children and of sailors…
biography: Nicholas was bishop of Myra in Lycia, in Asia Minor, in the early fourth century, and by tradition suffered imprisonment for the faith before the peace of the Church under Constantine. Little is known of his life with certainty, but he was venerated very early for his charity, above all for the story of his secret gift of gold that saved three poor girls from ruin.

His relics were carried to Bari in southern Italy in 1087, and his fame spread through the whole Church. From his hidden generosity grew, in many lands, the beloved figure of the Christmas gift-bringer.
saints.knownFor: Secret almsgiving that made him patron of children and sailors.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 6 December

saints.name: St. Ambrose
saints.title: Bishop and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: The governor acclaimed bishop of Milan by the people, who baptized Augustine and taught kings the limits of their power…
biography: Ambrose was a Roman governor at Milan when the people, still unbaptized as he was, acclaimed him their bishop; ordained within days, he gave away his goods and gave himself to study and preaching. He instructed and baptized St. Augustine, resisted the Arians and an emperor's overreach, and made Milan a center of Catholic life.
He composed hymns still sung and left many writings; he is one of the four great Latin Doctors of the Church.
saints.knownFor: Bishop of Milan, teacher of Augustine, Doctor of the Church.

canonization.canonized: Venerated from antiquity; Doctor of the Church

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 7 December

saints.name: The Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.title: Solemnity of the Blessed Virgin Mary
saints.shortBlurb: The Church honors Mary preserved from the first instant of her conception free from every stain of original sin…
biography: This solemnity celebrates the truth, defined as a dogma of the faith by Pope Pius IX in 1854, that the Blessed Virgin Mary was preserved from all stain of original sin from the very first moment of her conception, by a singular grace and in view of the merits of her Son. It is the Advent feast of the all-holy Mother made ready to bear the Lord.

Kept on 8 December, nine months before the feast of Mary's Nativity on 8 September, it is in many places a holy day of obligation, and under this title the Blessed Virgin is honored as the patroness of the United States.
saints.knownFor: Mary conceived without sin, the fitting dwelling prepared for the Son of God.

saints.name: St. Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin
saints.title: Layman and Seer of Guadalupe
saints.shortBlurb: The humble Indian convert of Mexico to whom the Virgin of Guadalupe appeared, leaving her image upon his cloak…
biography: Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin was a native of Mexico, baptized in his middle years by the first Franciscan missionaries. In December of 1531, on the hill of Tepeyac near Mexico City, the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared to him as a native woman and asked that a church be built there; when the bishop sought a sign, she filled his cloak with roses out of season, and on the cloak was found imprinted the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe.
Juan Diego spent his remaining years in prayer near the shrine, telling all who came of the Lady's message. His witness and the miraculous image drew millions of the native peoples to the faith.
saints.knownFor: The seer of Our Lady of Guadalupe, whose tilma bears her image.
patronage: the indigenous peoples of the Americas

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Juan Diego (vatican.va)

saints.name: St. Eulalia of Mérida
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A young girl of Roman Spain who defied the persecutors of Diocletian and was put to death for confessing Christ…
biography: Eulalia was a Christian girl of Mérida in Roman Spain who, during the persecution of Diocletian about the year 304, presented herself before the magistrate and boldly reproached him for compelling Christians to sacrifice to the gods. Though still very young, she would not yield, and she was tortured and burned to death.
Her memory was cherished throughout Spain and beyond; the poet Prudentius, within a century of her death, sang her passion in one of his hymns, and a great basilica rose over her tomb at Mérida.
saints.knownFor: One of the most celebrated virgin-martyrs of Roman Spain.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Damasus I
saints.title: Pope
saints.shortBlurb: The pope who set Jerome to work on the Latin Bible and adorned the tombs of the martyrs in the Roman catacombs…
biography: Damasus was born about 305 and served as a Roman deacon before his election as pope in 366. He defended the faith against Arianism and the errors of Apollinaris, upheld the primacy of the Roman See, and confirmed the teaching of the Council of Constantinople of 381.

He set his secretary St. Jerome to the revision of the Latin Scriptures that led in time to the Vulgate, and he sought out, restored, and adorned with verse inscriptions the graves of the martyrs in the catacombs. He died in 384.
saints.knownFor: Commissioning the Vulgate and honoring the martyrs of the catacombs.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 11 December

saints.name: Our Lady of Guadalupe
saints.title: Patroness of the Americas
saints.shortBlurb: The Mother of God, appearing on the hill of Tepeyac and leaving her image on a poor man's cloak, drew a whole people to Christ…
biography: In December of 1531, ten years after the Spanish conquest of Mexico, the Blessed Virgin Mary appeared to the Indian convert St. Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac, speaking to him in his own tongue and asking that a church be built there. As a sign for the doubting bishop, she caused roses to bloom in winter and left upon Juan Diego's cloak the image venerated ever since as Our Lady of Guadalupe.

The apparition and the miraculous image drew millions of the native peoples to baptism. Our Lady of Guadalupe was declared Patroness of Mexico and of all the Americas, and her shrine in Mexico City is among the most visited in the world.
saints.knownFor: Her apparition at Tepeyac and the miraculous image on the tilma.

saints.name: St. Lucy
saints.title: Virgin and Martyr
saints.shortBlurb: A virgin martyr of Syracuse in the persecution of Diocletian, honored as a bringer of light in the dark of winter…
biography: Lucy, a Christian maiden of Syracuse in Sicily, had vowed her virginity to God and gave her dowry to the poor. Betrayed in the persecution of Diocletian, she remained steadfast under threats and torture and was put to death about the year 304.
Her name means “light,” and her feast near the winter solstice made her a beloved bringer of light in the North; she is invoked by those with diseases of the eyes. Her name stands in the Roman Canon.
saints.knownFor: Her virgin martyrdom; patroness of the blind and of light.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 13 December

saints.name: St. John of the Cross
saints.title: Priest and Doctor of the Church
saints.shortBlurb: A Carmelite reformer and poet of the mystical life, who sang of the dark night of the soul and its union with God…
biography: John of the Cross joined the Carmelites and, with St. Teresa of Ávila, undertook the reform of the order, founding the Discalced friars. For this he suffered imprisonment at the hands of his own brethren, and it was in that cell that he began his greatest poetry. His works — the Ascent of Mount Carmel, the Dark Night, the Spiritual Canticle — are classics of mystical theology.
He died in 1591 and was declared a Doctor of the Church.
saints.knownFor: His mystical poetry and the reform of Carmel.

canonization.canonized: 1726 by Pope Benedict XIII; Doctor of the Church (1926)

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. John of the Cross”
Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 24 November

saints.name: St. Valerian of Abbenza
saints.title: Bishop and Confessor
saints.shortBlurb: An aged African bishop who, rather than surrender the goods of the Church to the Arian Vandals, was cast out to die in the open road…
biography: Valerian was bishop of Abbenza in Roman Africa during the Arian persecution waged by the Vandal king Genseric in the fifth century. Though he was more than eighty years old, he was commanded to hand over the sacred vessels and books of his church, and when he steadfastly refused, he was driven out of the city.

It was forbidden, on the king's order, that anyone shelter him in house or field, so that the old bishop lay a long time in the public road under the open sky, and there he ended his life as a confessor of the Catholic faith.
saints.knownFor: An aged confessor of the faith under the Arian Vandal persecution.

sources.text: The Roman Martyrology (1914 English ed.; public domain)

saints.name: St. Adelaide
saints.title: Empress
saints.shortBlurb: A queen imprisoned and delivered, empress of the Romans, who in widowhood gave herself to peace-making and the poor…
biography: Adelaide, born about 931, was daughter of the king of Burgundy and married young to the king of Italy. Widowed and then imprisoned by a usurper, she was rescued by Otto the Great of Germany, whom she married; she was crowned empress at Rome and became one of the most respected women of her age.

As mother and grandmother of emperors, and for a time regent, she used her influence for the peace of the realm, the reform of monasteries, and the relief of the poor. She retired at last near a convent she had founded and died in 999, honored as a saint.
saints.knownFor: Holy Roman Empress and benefactress of the Church.

canonization.canonized: Canonized in 1097 by Pope Urban II

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 16 December

saints.name: St. John of Matha
saints.title: Priest
saints.shortBlurb: A Paris theologian who founded an order to ransom Christians held captive by the Moors…
biography: John of Matha, born in Provence about 1160, studied at Paris and was ordained a priest. Moved by the plight of Christians enslaved by the Moors, he founded with St. Felix of Valois the Order of the Most Holy Trinity, approved by Pope Innocent III in 1198, whose members vowed to redeem captives, even offering themselves in exchange.
The Trinitarians spread through France, Spain, and North Africa, and over the centuries they, with the kindred Mercedarians, freed many thousands from bondage. John died at Rome in 1213.
saints.knownFor: Founding the Trinitarian Order for the ransom of captives.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 8 February

saints.name: St. Gatian of Tours
saints.title: First Bishop of Tours
saints.shortBlurb: One of the missionary bishops sent from Rome into Gaul, who planted the faith at Tours amid persecution…
biography: According to St. Gregory of Tours, Gatian was one of seven bishops sent from Rome about the middle of the third century to preach the Gospel in Gaul.
